speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
subtopic: INVESTIGATIVE INDEPENDENCE OF STANDING COMMITTEES- SPEAKER'S RULING
speechtext:
On November 26 the Hon. Member for Etobicoke North (Mr. Pennock) rose on a question of privilege relating to the investigative independence of standing committees. The Hon. Member couched his remarks in the context of the global implications for all committees. He referred to an incident between the Auditor General and the Standing Committee on Communications and Culture. Had the Hon. Member attempted to complain of the particular incident, I am afraid that the Chair would have had to quickly rule him out of order. It is a long standing principle that the Speaker does not intervene in matters which ought to be dealt with by the standing committees.

However, I allowed the Hon. Member for Etobicoke North (Mr. Pennock) to proceed because the Chair takes seriously any questions with a reference to the new Standing Orders adopted on February 14, 1986.
I think we must consider the problems arising from the application of the new Standing Orders if we are to make this experiment a success, and the Chair has an ongoing commitment to participating in the process as much as possible.

The specific issues raised by the Hon. Member for Etobicoke North are obviously well within the reach of the Standing Committee on Communications and Culture. I might add that the complaint referred to by the Hon. Member seems to be related to the new dynamics that are evolving in the relationship between the new standing committees and those departments and agencies that fall within their expanded mandates.
Time and experience will contribute to the education of the Canadian public, and of witnesses as to the new powers of the committees.

The matter is indeed a serious one, and I want to thank the Hon. Member for bringing it to the attention of the House, but for the time being, the Chair can find nothing that infringes on the privileges of Members or the prerogatives of the House.

In closing, may I say to the House that parliamentary reform is still an exploratory exercise, and some day it may well be up to the House to guarantee the authority of the Standing Committees, but it is firstly up to the standing committees to define their mandates, establish their independence, and publicize their expectations. When and if a standing committee reports back to the House that its work is being impeded, the Chair will not hesitate to intervene.
I wish to thank the Hon. Member for his intervention.

subtopic: COMMITTEE EXAMINATION OF ORDER IN COUNCIL APPOINTMENTS-SPEAKER'S RULING

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
subtopic: COMMITTEE EXAMINATION OF ORDER IN COUNCIL APPOINTMENTS-SPEAKER'S RULING
speechtext:
I am now ready to rule on the question of privilege raised on November 18 by the Hon. Member for Hamilton East (Ms. Copps), regarding the proceedings of the Standing Committee on Human Rights. The Hon. Member criticized the Committee's decision to reduce the number of witnesses proposed by its sub-committee. Instead of calling the sixteen witnesses proposed by the sub-committee, the Standing Committee decided that each Member could ask only one person appointed to the Canadian Human Rights Tribunal to appear before the Committee.

I have carefully considered the complaint raised by the Hon. Member, and the submissions which were made by Hon. Members on both sides of the argument. The discussion which took place clearly underlined the fact that a matter had been raised which was of great concern to the House. A number of procedures under which we are currently operating were only recently introduced on a provisional basis. Those relating to the powers of committees are of particular significance, and it is quite normal that Hon. Members would wish to air their concerns and clarify issues which could have far-reaching implications.
The Hon. Deputy Prime Minsiter (Mr. Mazankowski) in his contribution to the discussion reminded the House of the practice whereby the House cannot officially take notice of any committee proceedings except by way of a report from the committee concerned. He also referred to a relevant citation

December 16, 1986
Tabling of Documents
from Beauchesne's Fifth Edition. Citation 117(7) states as follows:
The opinion of the Speaker cannot be sought in the House about any matter arising or likely to arise in a committee.
Further confirmation is to be found in Citation 569(3) which states:
The Speaker has ruled on many occasions that it is not competent for him to exercise procedural control over the committees. Committees are and must remain masters of their own procedure.
Citation 608 goes on to state:
Procedural difficulties which arise in committees ought to be settled in the committee and not in the House.

The foregoing clearly indicates that the Chair cannot rule on a problem that arises in committee, unless it was reported by the committee to the House. It is also clear that a committee meeting that gives rise to a dispute does not constitute a valid question of privilege.

Having said that, I would immediately add that a question of such importance as that raised by the Hon. Member for Hamilton East is not one to be lightly dismissed. Her complaint arises from our political process and the political system under which we operate. Briefly stated, the power of decision is given to the majority. For protection the minority looks to the rules of procedure. The House is the master of its own procedure and can change it, including the procedure relating to the conduct of committees. I quote again from Beauchesne at Citation 569(2):
Committees receive their authority from the House itself and that authority of the House overrides that of any committee.
Thus, if Hon. Members are not satisfied with the present operation of Standing Order 104, or any other rules relating to committees, they should seek their remedies by way of procedural reform. I might add that that applies to Hon. Members on both sides of the House.

I therefore must rule that the question raised by the Hon. Member is not a question of privilege, but I do think the matter she raised deserves to be brought to the attention of the House.

speakeroldname: Hon. Tom Hockin (Minister of State (Finance)) moved
subtopic: EXCISE TAX ACT AND EXCISE ACT
speechtext:
that Bill C-14, an Act to amend the Excise Tax Act and the Excise Act, be read the third time and passed.
He said: Mr. Speaker, I will speak briefly, but first I would like to take this opportunity to thank Hon. Members of this Chamber for their assistance and consideration during the discussion and examination of Bill C-14.
This piece of legislation contains the necessary legislative authority to implement the sales and excise tax changes announced in the February, 1986 budget and the enrichments to the fuel tax rebate program for farmers announced by the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) in April, 1986. It provides authority for changes in the rates of federal sales taxes and excise taxes on alcohol and tobacco products which are intended to raise revenue in order to reduce the deficit.
The deficit affects us all and it threatens us all. Deficit reduction measures must be shared as broadly as possible. The Bill before you, Mr. Speaker, seeks to achieve this objective by spreading the tax increases broadly and fairly. To ensure that all Canadians will contribute in an equitable manner, a new refundable sales tax credit of $50 per adult and $25 per child will be available for lower income Canadians to help offset the 1 percentage point increase in the sales tax rates implemented by this Bill.
During consideration of this Bill by the Legislative Committee, concerns were raised about the adequacy of this new tax credit. This is an important issue and I respect Members raising it. I would like to take an opportunity to address it very briefly. First, let us not forget that this refundable sales tax credit represents a unique and important initiative and clearly demonstrates the Government's concern for low income Canadians. It is the first time in our history that the federal Government has provided an income tested refundable tax credit for low income Canadian families whether or not they have children.
In designing the credit, foremost in the Government's concern was to protect those who could least afford to absorb the increase in the federal sales tax. Given the Government's limited resources, and we all know they are limited, it was impossible to design a credit that would offset the increased tax burden exactly by family size and income level. I believe that the $15,000 income threshold beyond which benefits are gradually reduced achieves an ideal balance in terms of maximizing the size of the credit and the number of beneficiaries, within an acceptable fiscal framework, while ensuring that Canadians in the lowest income brackets are fully protected against the increase in the federal sales tax. Indeed, this credit overcompensates individuals earning less than $15,000 annually.
The measures in this Bill to enrich the fuel tax rebate program are of particular benefit to farmers. First, a one year extension of the over-all fuel tax rebate program will provide additional benefits amounting to $120 million in 1987 for all primary producers, including farmers. In addition, farmers will be entitled to an additional 2.5 cents a litre rebate to relieve them fully of the sales and excise taxes on gasoline and diesel fuel. This will be further increased to 3.5 cents on January 1, 1987 to conincide with a 1 cent increase in the excise tax currently scheduled for that date. These enrichments for farmers will provide additional assistance totalling $165 million. Over 200,000 Canadian farmers will benefit under this program. These measures clearly reflect the Government's concern for the economic situation confronting farmers.
In the coming year the net impact of these changes will be to reduce the deficit by approximately $1 billion. It should be noted, however, that for every $1 that taxes have been increased to reduce the deficit, expenditures have been cut by $3. Let me emphasize that, Mr. Speaker; for every $1 that taxes have been increased to reduce the deficit, federal Government expenditures have been cut by $3. Our policies to wrestle the deficit and manage the Government better are part of a comprehensive set of actions to deal with a wide range of economic and fiscal needs.
In conclusion, together, the tax changes and expenditure cuts are an important and fair way of restoring fiscal order to this country. All Canadians will benefit from the successful achievement of these goals.

Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to have the opportunity to participate in this debate. While we have been debating this Bill for some days now in the House of Commons, Members of this House still have some grave reservations about the effect of Bill C-14. We have raised those concerns in the House in the past and this morning I will try to summarize some of the issues that my colleagues and I have brought to your attention during the last few weeks, Mr. Speaker. This is not a very voluminous piece of legislation. It has only 15 pages or so, but the consequences of the Bill are very serious to the people upon whom we are called to represent in this House.

Mr. Speaker, if and when this Bill is passed, there will be an increase in the federal sales tax on manufactured goods; increases in the price of wine, tobacco, beer, and spirits; and increases in the Air Transportation Tax and the Telecommunication Programming Services Tax. There is also the fuel tax question and other increases that will have a disastrous effect on the tourist industry, as, I am sure my hon. friend from Westmorland-Kent (Mr. Robichaud) will agree. Finally, there are the sales and excise taxes on motor fuel that will be refundable to diplomats, the collection of income tax in Canada, the fuel tax rebate for farmers, and the impact of measures related to sales tax and excise tax on the federal
December 16, 1986

Government's revenues, all of which deserve consideration this morning.

We must remember that the Minister of State for Finance (Mr. Hockin) has just told us that the Bill is designed to spread the burden fairly among Canadians, or words to that effect, if I can paraphrase what the Minister said. If one looks closely at the effect of this Bill, Mr. Speaker, you will notice that it does not do that at all, and I ask the Minister to address it in the future.
He said that his Bill is fair. I ask him about a one earner couple with two children whose income is $15,000 a year. This couple will have a tax increase of 1.7 per cent or will pay an extra $255 in tax increases as a result of the February, 1986 Budget, the November, 1984 Economic Statement and the May, 1985 Budget. The combination of the three Conservative budgetary documents will create that situation. I ask the Minister what is fair about imposing that kind of an extra burden on a family of four earning $15,000 a year? That family does not have one extra cent to give to the Government, much less $255 more in taxes.
I draw to your attention the fact that a one income couple with two children, with a total family income of $50,000 a year, will be asked to pay 1.2 per cent more in taxes. It is a 1.7 per cent increase for the first family and 1.2 per cent for the second family. That hardly sounds fair. Yet the Minister tells us this is fair legislation.

Mr. Speaker, take for instance an elderly couple with an annual income of $27,000, which has to spend 1.9 per cent more because of the measures contained in three Budgets: the economic statement of November 1984, the 1985 Budget and the 1986 Budget, which all add up to an increase of 1.9 per cent in expenses for an elderly couple with an annual income of $27,000.
Mr. Speaker, I don't think that is what we call justice. [English]
I hear a Conservative Member saying "Not bad when they get an increase at the same time". He may think it is fair that low-income people are asked to pay a greater percentage in taxes than those who earn a great deal more. I do not think it is fair at all.
If the Government was asking Canadians equally to sacrifice, and it was at least fair for all, it would not be all that hard to swallow. If the Government followed its own prescription it would be even easier. Yet the Government is telling ordinary Canadians that times are tough and they are going to have to cut down on expenditures and expectations. They are going to have to cut down on what they receive, and give the Government more in taxes. If the Government said that and practised what it preached it would not be quite as bad.

Remember, that was only one-eighth of the waste we have now. He said:
How can a Government call on a nation to restrain itself and to be more realistic in its collective demands upon our economy when its own record is an unbroken string of fiscal excess? Canadians may be many things but stupid we are not. We simply will not buy leadership that so blatantly has one code of conduct for itself and quite a different one for the rest of us.
Do you know who said that? I just told you a minute ago. It is the author of the book Where 1 Stand who said that to the people of Canada. Although I do not recommend buying the book, I am sure people can go to a library and view it for a moment. It would probably be cheaper. They could then see where the Prime Minister stood at the time he was Leader of the Opposition, at the time he wrote this book, at the time he so sanctimoniously told the people of Canada that the preceding Government was not as accountable as it could be to the people of Canada. Probably no Government is as accountable as it should be. We are not suggesting that any previous Government ever was. The author of the book Where I Stand talks about the fiscal excess of the previous Government. That excess has been increased eight times in two years. When something which is unacceptable is multiplied eight times, it is eight times more unacceptable.
It is important that we hold the Government accountable for its fiscal excess. We must hold the Government accountable when it asks the House for money, as it is through this Bill. It is asking for more money with which to administer the Government. Collectively we must learn what the Government is going to do with this money and only then decide whether the Government should have it.
A Member across the way indicated a while ago that my remarks were not entirely relevant to the debate. I believe that when the Government asks for more money it is relevant to point out how it administered the money we previously gave it. If our children ask us for an excessive amount of money, it is normal to ask how they spent the money we already gave them. That is what I am doing today. I am asking the Government what it did with the money we gave it before. Members of Parliament give the Government its money. We give the Government the money of our constituents. No Government has any money of its own. Governments administer the money of the people. Therefore it is important to hold the Government accountable for what I consider to be fiscal excess.
I will quote again from the article to which I referred previously. It continues:
Mulroney was put up in a S3,400-a-night suite in the Plaza-Athenee Hotel in Paris this February. Trudeau paid $1,250 for his room in the Ritz when he last visited Paris on a peace mission in 1983.

Mulroney's entourage of 24 spent more than $11,000 for limousines to get around New York-

Trudeau's party of 11 ran up just over $2,000 in limousine bills-in January, 1984.

Canadians are asked to pay for such fiscal excess. The tax increases which the Government wishes to levy are unfair. There is no good reason for levying these taxes because the Government has an unbroken string of fiscal excess.

Mr. Speaker, Canadians are sick and tired of all this. It is hardly a coincidence that public opinion polls clearly show the Prime Minister's popularity and that of his Government has sagged considerably. Look at the Port-Cartier affair: $41 million completely wasted, Mr. Speaker. And why, I ask Hon. Members opposite: Why do they waste money like this?
The Minister of Supply and Services (Mrs. Vezina) sitting opposite is responsible for awarding certain contracts, but in the case of Port-Cartier, it was her predecessor. Yesterday we realized he did not do a very good job, because in the process, it seems to have been a conflict of interest, so that the contractor had to be released.
And the wasteful spending goes on: $41 million spent for no good reason. A penitentiary is being built in a part of the country where it isn't needed, at any rate not for prisoners. It may be needed as a stimulus for regional development, but there is certainly no justification for building a prison. Perhaps for building another Government building, but certainly not for building a prison, because we don't need one. Furthermore, we have to consider the cost of bringing prisoners to this institution when it is completed. How much will that cost? Imagine, the cost of putting the guards on the plane and taking these people down there, with their legal advisers, to Port-Cartier.
And finally the other point which people have a tendency to forget, Mr. Speaker, is that the inmate may be in jail, but his wife and children are not. Most prisoners will come from the Montreal area, so the families of prisoners will have no choice but to board a bus, pay $210 for return fares to Port-Cartier, and sit for 34 hours on that bus just to go and visit a family member.
I do not know whether I understood correctly, I do not know whether the Minister did say they live in Baie-Comeau, but I hope this is not what she said about prisoners' families, because they are quite free to live where they want. The fact is that most of them do not live there, quite a number come from the Montreal area.

Mr. Speaker, I wish to add a few remarks to this debate on Bill C-14. It has been debated on other occasions, both in committee and in the House, but I think it is worth some further comment before the House moves on to other business.
I am sure most Members are aware that Bill C-14 increases the sales and excise taxes that the Government charges on numerous manufactured goods and other items such as alcohol and tobacco. It is one of a series of tax increases that the Conservative Government has imposed since it was elected in 1984.
Many Canadians may not be aware that the Conservative Government has increasingly relied on increases in sales and excise taxes as a means of gaining more revenue than previously had been the case. The total taxes that the average Canadian family pays the Government will have increased by some $1,230 since the 1984 election of the Conservative Government. Of that amount, the average Canadian family will pay $385 more in increased income tax which constitutes around 31 per cent of the increase in taxes. They will be paying $845 more in sales and excise tax and that constitutes some 69 per cent of their taxes.
The thing about sales taxes, of course, is that they are hidden. One does not see them when they are included in the sale price. When a person buys manufactured goods, the 12
per cent the federal Government charges, and in some cases it might be a little less, is hidden in that price so that the consumer never knows how much he is actually paying in taxes. The Government is nickel and diming the taxpayers.
The Conservative Government has increased the number of items which are applicable for sales tax. It has expanded the federal sales tax in previous Budgets to include things such as vitamins, some non-prescription drugs, candy bars, softdrinks and a whole host of items which were never taxed previously. This Government, as I mentioned before, is relying more and more on the sales tax as a way of increasing public revenue. It does that because the Canadian taxpayer is not aware he or she is paying these new taxes.
Let us look at the taxes the Government has imposed since being elected in 1984. It has increased taxes through sales and excise taxes by some $6.7 billion. Personal income taxes have increased by some $3.3 billion and corporate taxes have increased by $1.4 billion. Again, these figures illustrate the Government's dependence upon increases in sales and excise taxes as a major revenue grab from the taxpayers' pockets.
We object to the increases in sales and excise taxes for several reasons. First, it is not progressive. It does not mean that the tax load is carried by those who are in a better position to pay the tax. It means people who are the least capable of carrying the tax load are penalized. The regressive nature of the tax can be seen when one looks at the various income groups and understands what the increases in sales and excise taxes since 1984 mean to them.
It is true that a family earning $15,000 a year or less will receive a rebate of $150, which is $50 for every adult 18 years of age and over and $25 a year for every child. That means an average family of four will get back $150. Of course, the $150 does not cover the total increase in sales and excise taxes the family will have to pay. It will be worse off. The family earning $10,000 a year or less will in fact pay an increase in taxes of some 0.2 per cent. A family earning $15,000 a year will pay a net increase of 0.4 per cent in new taxes. Even the very, very poor who will receive a tax rebate of $150 will still see the amount of money it pays in taxes increase because of the Conservative Budget. However, the people who get hit the hardest are the working poor, for example, the family of four which earns some $20,000 a year. That income is still well below the poverty line for many families living in larger centres. The couple earning a net family income of $20,000 per year with two children will pay an extra $269 per year in extra taxes through the sales and excise taxes. That is a 1.3 per cent increase in taxes going out of the family income.
We can look as well at the well-to-do families and find that that family pays a smaller percentage of the family income in sales and excise taxes. For example, for a family with a total income of $100,000 a year, the net cost as a percentage of family income going to tax is only 0.9 per cent. Therefore, a family with $20,000 in income pays 1.3 per cent of the family income in this new tax whereas the family earning $100,000 a
December 16, 1986

year only sees 0.9 per cent of its family income going to this new tax.
The sales tax is regressive. It is not fair. It taxes those who are the least capable of affording these taxes. It is not a tax based one's ability to pay. These taxes penalize people, not in accordance with their means to pay but regardless of their means to pay.
At this Christmas time of year one must wonder how some families can afford Christmas gifts, Christmas trees and the extra food their children expect and hope for. I do not believe the Government and those people in the Department of Finance have any idea of how millions of Canadians live. They do not realize the economic hardship which exists and the difficulties which are faced day in and day out as these people try to make ends meet. I do not believe the Government, and those people in Finance who devise these master schemes for raising more money, have any idea what it is like for a wage earner who has been laid off and is now existing on employment insurance. He has children to feed, clothe and house. They do not understand the careful planning and budgeting these people must do and the difficult decisions they must make day-in and day-out as to where to spend their money. There is an amazing amount of preoccupation in the budgeting of their meagre incomes. The Government and the Department of Finance have no notion what millions of Canadians experience day-in and day-out.
When we see the type of legislation such as C-14, legislation that increases the tax load on these people, we can only conclude that not only are these measures unfair but that they are indecent. They are uncaring and bereft of any understanding and compassion for those who have to struggle on a daily basis in order to survive. It is not just a few lazy bums who have difficulty budgeting. There are millions of Canadians who find themselves in such circumstances.
The number of people who will be eligible for the $150 tax rebate is 3.4 million. These are families of four with incomes of less than $15,000 per year. These 3.4 million families will receive some redress in the form of the $150 tax rebate. However, they, too, will be paying more in taxes than they were paying before because of the sales and excise tax measures.
One can think of the millions of people who are earning between $18,000 and $22,000 per year who are trying to raise children and who will not be eligible for any rebate at all. Instead, they will be paying hundreds of dollars more in taxes because of the sales and excise tax. They will experience tremendous difficulties, particularly in the Christmas season.
When one considers the totality of the budgetary items that the Government has introduced since its election one finds that the Government has hit the poor and the middle income earners more than it has hit anyone else. To its list of taxpayers it has added hundreds and thousands of people who were so
Excise Tax Act
poor before that they were not paying taxes. However, they will now be paying income tax because of the various measures introduced by the Government.
When we consider the statistics, and we will have more to say about this when Bill C-23 comes forward for debate, we will show that those with low and middle incomes are the ones who are taking the brunt of the Government's revenue grab. We will show that high income earners will be paying less than they have been paying in the past because of the various tax measures and loopholes that the Government has afforded the well-to-do. We will also show that the corporate sector, those who have been doing quite well, will continue with the tax holidays they received under the previous Liberal Government and under the present Conservative Government. The inequities and unfairness in our tax system would make an honest person blush. Unfortunately, we do not have a Government that knows how to blush.
One must question the economic wisdom of taxing consumption as opposed to income. Not only is it unfair because it hits the poor more than it hits the well-to-do, but it relies increasingly on tax on consumption rather than income. We know that economic recovery means that people have dollars in their pockets which they are able to spend on goods and services, which in turn creates jobs. If taxes on consumption are increased then spending is discouraged. If spending is discouraged, then surely the demand for goods and services is discouraged which, in turn, loses jobs. I am not certain that the Government and the people in the Department of Finance fully appreciate what they are doing when they increase the sales and excise taxes. Nor are they aware of the effect it will have on inflation, consumer spending and employment. I do not think the Government fully understands the economic implications of these tax measures.
The last point I wish to make concerns the over-all justification for increasing these taxes which Conservatives offer in the House. Earlier this morning we heard the Minister of State for Finance (Mr. Hockin) justify, in essence, the increase in taxes on the basis of fighting the deficit. In essence, the Government is telling the Canadian people, we are sorry but we have to increase your taxes because we have to knock the deficit down. I for one do not disagree with reducing the deficit. I think the deficit has to be reduced. It is obscene that we have so much owing, that so much of our revenue that is collected every year has to go to pay off the interest on the deficit.
Where I disagree with the Government is in its understanding of the cause of the deficit and the measures taken to fight it. The reason for the deficit is that the Government and the previous Liberal Government allowed so many tax loopholes that the well-to-do and, in particular, the large and prosperous corporations have not had to pay their fair share in taxes. The tax loss has been tremendous-in fact, it is horrendous. Billions of dollars have been lost. Taxes which should have been collected have not been collected because of various loopholes.

I have used the following example in the House before. However, I will use it again because often when one repeats a point over and over again it eventually sinks in. I wish to illustrate the point that those who should have been paying have not been paying with the following example. A female teller with the Royal Bank of Canada will have paid more in actual dollars and cents in taxes in the year 1982 than the Royal Bank of Canada paid in 1982. In fact, the Royal Bank of Canada made over $300 million in profits and it did not pay one cent in tax. In fact, it received a tax credit of some $6 million. It is no wonder we have the deficit that we do. It is no wonder that the kid who pumps gas for Shell paid more dollars and cents in taxes in 1982 than did Shell Oil, even though Shell Oil made millions of dollars in profits in 1982. It is no wonder we have the deficit.
We in the New Democratic Party claim that if we are going to fight the deficit it must not be done on the backs of the working poor. It is criminal to charge an extra $200 or $300 to the person earning $20,000 who is trying to raise a family. Let the Royal Bank of Canada, Imperial Oil, and Shell Canada start paying their fair share. Perhaps then we can begin to reduce the deficit and bring some economic and fiscal responsibility and morality to this country.

Mr. Speaker, I only wish to make a few comments and will not take the full 20 minutes. The Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson) in the House on several occasions has promised fiscal changes and reforms to make a more progressive and a fairer taxation system for ordinary Canadians. If we were to comment on the actions of the Government in the last two years, it would be found that instead of fair tax system, there is a tax system which bears more heavily on the lower and middle income people than it did before.
During the first two years of the Conservative Government, instead of introducing the fairer tax system it implemented a tax system which is much less fair than the previous one. There were many problems in the tax system before this Government came to power, but it has not done anything to improve the system. For example, the changes that this Government has brought in since September of 1984 have increased taxes by $1,300 for the average Canadian family. It has increased taxes for the ordinary Canadian by adding heavily to excise and sales taxes, instead of using personal taxes. That is a regressive tax, and it is exactly the opposite to what the Government said it would do.
In the November, 1984 Economic Statement the increase in sales and excise taxes added another $350 per year for the average family. In the May, 1985 Budget the Government again imposed a 1 per cent sales tax which cost the ordinary Canadian an average of $325 per year. Finally, in February, 1986 another $170 was added, not necessarily in income tax, but in taxes paid by the ordinary Canadian. Adding all those
taxes up totals an increase of $845 per year. All this has been done in two years.
During the same period income tax increases, which are supposedly more progressive and equitable for families whose financial circumstances can vary considerably, have totalled only $385 per year, compared to $845 added by excise and sales taxes. In the last two years 69 per cent of the tax increases were covered by excise and sales taxes, and only 31 per cent by income taxes. In other words, this Government is opting for unfair and regressive tax, and not for fair taxes which will even out the structure of the tax system.
The Government has been stating that it will close the loopholes and cut personal income taxes so that the middle or lower income people will receive a better break. Most of the low income people, and many of the middle income people, do not have any loopholes. So plugging those loopholes will not help them at all. The cuts that the Government has put in place have not been in the lower tax areas, they have been in the marginal and the upper tax areas. Instead of benefiting the poorer people, the taxes that have been put in place are benefiting only the rich.
It is important to keep reminding the Government that its direction is exactly opposite to what it promised when it was elected. It is exactly opposite to what it says every time the Minister of Finance stands in the House and proclaims that he is making changes in taxes. It is rather sad to realize that most of the taxes that have been put before the House are not up front for everybody to see. In a sense this Government is not being honest, because it is hiding the taxes. The Government is not being accountable for the taxes it is putting on.
This Bill levies a series of taxes which are almost under the table type of taxes. People do not recognize that they are paying them, and consequently the Government does not have to take the political heat for putting these taxes in place. When most people pay excise and sales taxes they are unaware that they are paying a tax. Consequently, they do not react to them in the same way that they would to income taxes, which are much more progressive.
So we have a Government that opts for regressive taxes for its own benefit, even while it stands in the House and suggests that what it intends to do is make a fairer and better tax system which will not tax the lower and lower middle income people, but will increase taxes on the corporations and the higher income people.
I suggest that even as this Bill goes through the Government is using the cowardly approach. It is not dealing with fair taxation, but it is allowing its political hopes for the future to be based on the type of taxation which people will not recognize, not know that they are paying. If you have a very low income, you pay an inordinate amount of that income in taxation through sales and excise taxes. You may not pay very much in income tax if you have a very low income, but if you have a high income you pay a very small part of that income in sales and excise taxes. That is why these types of taxes should

be avoided, and we should be looking at a fair taxation system which has a more equitable effect on all Canadians.

Mr. Speaker, I am quite delighted to have an opportunity today to make some comments on Bill C-14, an Act to amend the Excise Tax Act and the Excise Act. Some very important points must be put on record.
At the outset I indicate that because of the time of year we all make efforts to expedite and facilitate the business of the House. This is probably the last speech we will make on the particular Bill. I say that so people can make their plans for Bill C-23, the back-up Bill. Unfortunately it is another tax Bill on top of the Bill which we are debating at the moment. It will see more increases in taxation.
It is important for Canadians to know that since the Conservatives formed the Government of Canada, starting in September, 1984, they have introduced an incredible number of new taxes. The ordinary Canadian family is now taxed significantly greater than it was prior to the election of the Conservative Government. As a matter of fact, if we add tax increases experienced by the ordinary Canadian family, in addition to already being overburdened with taxation, the Conservative taxes amount to $1,350 per family. That is an increase on top of the other taxes the family already pays.
For the purpose of this example, we are assuming that the average Canadian family is a family of four, including two dependent children, with a combined income of $35,000. I realize that in many parts of Canada that is not a typical family income. However, when we look statistically across Canada and include the more prosperous areas and the regions of Canada, we come up with an average family income of about $35,000.
There has been a variety of new taxes such as increased taxes on construction materials for home building and such goods, increased taxes on manufactured items, increased gasoline taxes, increased sales taxes on a variety of items, increased taxes on commodities, and increased taxes on alcoholic beverages, cable and pay television services, tobacco products, and so on. It averages, as I said, $1,350 per Canadian family. I call them Conservative taxes because they are taxes imposed by the Conservative Government. It is important for Canadians to know those facts.
My recollection of the last federal election campaign was that the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney), who was then the Leader of the Conservative Party, indicated that they should get Government off the backs of Canadians; that was the theme on various Canadian streets. Many people assumed that to mean that taxes would be lessened, that the burden of taxes on their backs would be lessened. They thought that that meant a reduction in taxes paid at the gas pumps, in stores and shops, and in the factories of Canada. However, that was not the case. As a result of various economic statements and
Excise Tax Act
Budgets introduced by the Conservative Government, we have actually seen an increase in taxes.
As a matter of fact, the biggest surprise occurred just yesterday when the Minister responsible for regulations tabled a 637 page report in the House. It contained proposed new rules on everything from the quality of orange juice concentrate to Canadian content on country music radio stations. They talk about the need to get the Government off the backs of Canadian citizens, yet they bring in 637 pages of federal rules on everything. As a matter of fact, the report itself weighs 1.5 kilograms. It is a massive document which shows that we are regulated in every aspect of our lives.
If I refer to my speech notes on Bill C-14, it looks like there will be more and more taxes. Surely to goodness there is an end. Surely to goodness they cannot keep increasing taxes.
I should like to refer to the May, 1985 Budget of the Minister of Finance. In that one statement alone he increased the federal sales tax by 1 per cent. He increased the tax on gasoline by two cents per litre effective September 3, 1985 and by one cent per litre effective January 1, 1986. He also said that there would be a new tax of two cents per litre on diesel and aviation fuels. He broadened the federal sales tax to include candies, soft drinks, pet foods, certain kinds of health foods, certain kinds of energy conservation equipment, and the like. Then he went on to say that the excise tax on tobacco would be increased by 52 per cent and that the excise tax on alcohol would be increased by 2 per cent. That was just in the May, 1985 Budget.
I should now like to refer to the November, 1984 Economic Statement. Again the Government announced another 1 per cent federal sales tax increase and an increase in the petroleum compensation charge. Most recently, in the February, 1986 Budget, it announced another 1 per cent federal sales tax increase for April 1, 1986, an excise tax increase on tobacco of another 6 per cent, and an excise tax increase on alcohol of 4 per cent. It goes on and on. There are literally pages and pages of increased taxes. Surely there is a limit.
A few months ago the Minister of Finance stood in his place and said that the tax system had to be changed, that it had to be improved. Many Canadians thought that that meant reduced amounts of taxes or that the tax system would be made simpler, or whatever. However, that is not the case. The Minister of Finance now wants to introduce a new set of tax regulations called the business transfer tax where everything will be taxed in every business transfer. This means that if one goes to a lawyer to write up a will for the benefit of one's children, spouse, other members of the family or friends, if one picks up one's laundry or if one goes out bowling for the evening, one will be paying new federal taxes.
I think Canadians have been pushed to the absolute brink by expecting them to pay a new set of taxes enthusiastically. I suspect a tax revolt is in the offing. When the Minister of Finance tables the details of the business transfer tax, people will realize that they will pay hundreds of dollars in increased

December 16, 1986
Excise Tax Act
taxes on areas which were not taxed in the past. They will say, we have had it. Enough is enough. We are mad as hell. We will not take it any more. We will not continue to pay taxes.
We see this reaction against unfair Canadian tax laws every day-the underground economy. Many billions of dollars in transactions go untaxed every year because people have lost faith in the tax system. They have lost faith in the ability of the Government to introduce a fair tax. Transactions involving billions of dollars take place underground. They are never reported and thereby people avoid paying tax to various jurisdictions. The barter system takes place and cash is passed under the table. I suspect Members of Parliament would have to admit that they are aware of the underground economies in neighbourhoods and communities. It is in the forefront. People ask, why should I pay taxes to the Conservative Government in Ottawa which does not even tax thousands of profitable corporations?
According to my last recollection, if we add up the number of profitable corporations in Canada which do not even pay a single cent in federal income tax, it totals almost 80,000. That is almost inconceivable to an average person working in an office, a mine, a mill, or a small business. Such persons pay taxes on every paycheque. They can look at their paycheques and see what they are paying in personal income taxes. They see that they are paying thousands of dollars every year, yet they know about these 80,000 large corporations.
I should like to be specific and refer to some of them. They include the Bank of Montreal, the Royal Bank of Canada, General Motors, Nova Corporation, Hudson's Bay Company, and Shell Oil. I could list 80,000 of those corporations that make profits year after year after year. Sometimes they make in excess of hundreds of millions of dollars of profits. In 1983 the Royal Bank of Canada made in excess of $300 million in profits and did not pay a single cent in income tax. That was the same year the Bank of Montreal made just about $300 million in profits and it did not pay a single cent in income tax. The Hudson's Bay Company that year I think made just under $100 million in profits and did not pay one single cent in income tax.
Canadians say that is unfair and unjust. It is not right and consequently Canadians are getting more and more reluctant to pay what the Government says is "your fair share" knowing that all of these other large corporations have paid zip for many years. That says nothing about the many wealthy individuals who obtain incomes from a variety of investment sources and are able to manipulate the way they conduct their financial affairs in order to pay no income tax year after year after year.
The Government said it brought in a minimum tax and I should remember that. I do remember that, Mr. Speaker. I also remember receiving in the mail an example of a letter that went out from one of the largest accounting firms in Canada saying, here are six differrent routes you can use in your
financial affairs to avoid paying even the minimum tax. Already the creative accountants, tax lawyers and tax accountants have found ways and means of getting around the so-called minimum tax.
It is a very sad situation when we find once again that the Government is coming to Parliament saying, we must pass this Bill to collect even more taxes from Canadians. What kind of a Bill is this, Mr. Speaker? It is a Bill that will result in increased federal sales and excise taxes. If you look at what has happened in Canada since the Conservatives took over Government, sales and excise taxes have increased $6.7 billion in terms of adding money to the federal coffers. That money has been taken out of the hands, the wallets, purses and pocket-books of Canadian citizens through sales and excise taxes.
I know, Mr. Speaker, that you are the kind of fellow who would probably ask, I wonder what else has been collected? How does that compare to personal and corporate taxes?" If you look at corporate income taxes, it does not even begin to come close to the $6.7 billion which has come from sales and excise taxes. Corporate taxes increased by only $1.4 billion. What about personal taxes? They went up $3.3 billion. We all know when you talk about sales tax that it is in a sense a hidden tax. People pay gasoline taxes at the gas pumps. When you look at sales and excise taxes and combine them with the increase in personal income tax the money collected totals nearly $10 billion more.
These are Conservative taxes that now add up to $10 billion more taken out of the small communities, towns and cities for use by the federal Government for some highly questionable things. I suppose someone has to pay the extra $41 million so we can build a prison in the Prime Minister's constituency. That is where this money goes. That is why people are outraged at being manipulated and used in such an exploitive way.
On the other hand, I suppose a lot of people will say that is all right and fine, surely we have to raise money to conduct the affairs of Canada. Indeed, we do. But should we collect it from sales and excise taxes or should we collect it through a progressive tax system of personal and corporate taxes?
As New Democrats we oppose Bill C-14 because we feel that sales taxes and excise taxes are the wrong way to raise revenues, for a variety of reasons. Let me mention two or three. First, these are hidden, sneaky, sleazy, underhanded under the table type of taxes. No one knows he or she is paying them. When you buy a product manufactured in Canada and you know there are significant increases in manufacturers' sales tax, those increases are not shown in the price of that product. People do not know to what extent the federal Government is gouging them in this under-the-table, sneaky fashion. They assume this is the price of the product of the developers, manufacturers, retailers or wholesalers. But this sneaky tax is also being added, and once again in Bill C-14 the federal Government is increasing it. We do not like it because it is not an honest tax in the sense that it is not up front for
December 16, 1986

everyone to see. The federal Government uses this method because it can keep the tax under the table and out of the view of Canadian citizens. We say that is wrong. It is not democratic and it is not forthright. It is sneaky as far as the Government is concerned.
Second, we do not like this tax because it is very regressive. When the very wealthy Canadian buys his or her snow tires he or she might have to pay an extra sales tax now of let us say $5. They do not even notice the $5 as an increase in the cost of a set of snow tires. But when a person from a very poor family goes in to buy that set of snow tires, which you must have in Canada, that person pays the same $5 extra in sales tax but it hurts. The poor family notices the significant erosion of the money at his disposal when he has to pay an extra $5, $10 or $12 through sales taxes. When that person buys his gasoline at the pump it costs an extra $2 or $3 because of increased gasoline taxes. That really hurts the family on a limited income, for example, the veteran on a veteran's pension, the senior citizen on a fixed income, a working family with a very low annual income. But it does not hurt the upper income earner. It does not hurt the person who is obtaining his or her income from investments in the $150,000 to $200,000 salary range. Those people do not notice it. Not only is it a sneaky tax because you cannot see it, it is unfair in that it hurts the low-income earner much more than it hurts the upper-income earner. A millionaire certainly does not worry much about paying sales tax, but the poor family certainly does.
Third, we oppose this type of unfair hidden tax because it is a toll on the consumer and, therefore, it retards the possibility of economic development and expansion in economic areas and job creation. When you take $6, $7, $8 or $9 billion out of the small towns, cities and rural areas of Canada through the taxation system, those dollars are not in those communities to circulate. Those dollars are not being spent at the local barber shop, the local service station or at the local shop down the road. Those dollars are dragged to Ottawa to be spent on priorities that the Government of Canada might have in building new embassies, in some cases, or deciding where to build prisons and that type of thing. Those dollars are not circulating time and time again throughout the year in these small communities. What does that do to the small shop owner, the small business person running a store or a small factory? It means that growth does not take place at the same rate. The consumer has less disposable income.
The most recent quarterly economic review published by the Department of Finance shows that during April and May of this year the disposable income of Canadians fell by 2 per cent. The Conference Board says that our ability to buy is becoming less and less. The National Council on Welfare goes on at some length in its report indicating that it is the middle and low-income Canadians who have less and less disposable income, a situation which harms the economy. Our type of economy requires people to buy services and goods and when they stop or they do not do it at the same rate it slows the economy. That is why in many cases we have such a sluggish
Excise Tax Act
economic recovery, if there is an economic recovery occurring at all in some regions.
Given that it retards growth and is a hidden, regressive tax, we feel Bill C-14 should not go ahead. What should go ahead is a commitment by the Government to begin a thorough and complete tax reform. It should make our tax system fair, just and equitable. It should collect a reasonable amount of the tax burden from the corporate sector and get away from the imposition of sales or excise taxes which by definition are unfair, unjust and, quite frankly, un-Canadian.

The curious thing about the federal Conservative Government is that on the one hand pressure has been put on various programs, as exemplified in the spring of 1985 by its attempt to deindex Old Age Security and the carrying through in the fall with deindexation of family allowances. subsubtopic: PLIGHT OF DOMINION COAL COMPANY OF CANADA RETIREES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise today to urge the Government of Canada to acknowledge its moral responsibility to the retired workers of the Dominion Coal Company of Canada. These individuals worked for the coal mining company which has since become the Cape Breton Development Corporation. These men provided many years of fine service to this company but have never received any sort of pension income after their retirement.
December 16, 1986

As a consequence of this, Mr. Speaker, a great many of my constituents are living well below the poverty line of $12,500 for a couple living in a small town. That figure comes from the National Council of Welfare. Some people may think that this could not happen in a country like Canada. However, if we take the time to look at the specific case of one miner, we see that a man who has worked in the mines for 35 years must support himself and his elderly wife on no more than $637.96 a month. This amounts to less than $7,700 a year and, tragically, is well below the poverty line.
A Government's compassion is measured by the way it supports and assists the poor and the weak. If the Government has an ounce of compassion, it will acknowledge immediately that it has a moral responsibility to provide assistance to the former employees of the Dominion Coal Company of Canada and allow them to live out the rest of their lives in quiet dignity. I urge the Government and the Cape Breton Development Corporation to move on this matter forthwith.

Mr. Speaker, have you ever gone to the doctor knowing that he or she was not allowed to tell you you were sick, even if you were? This is what the Government did with the task force examining the cuts at the National Research Coucil.

subtopic: CRUISE MISSILE TESTING-STUDENT'S LETTER TO PRIME MINISTER
CRUISE MISSILE TESTING-STUDENT'S LETTER TO PRIME MINISTER
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, at this time of year it is common to hear wishes of peace on earth, good will to all people. I am pleased to say I have received a great many letters from students at John Gunn Junior High in my riding. They have written to me and to the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) with respect to their concern about the future of the world.
I would like to read a few lines from a letter which was sent to the Prime Minister from a student at John Gunn Junior High:
I am writing this letter because I am concerned over what nuclear war would do to my future and the future of the world.
I am scared about what nuclear arms will do to me, my family and my friends. I want to live a full life but with this threat of a nuclear war hanging over my head, I wonder if I will.
She goes on to say to the Prime Minister:
What I expect of you is to take this letter very seriously. I am only a teenager, you are an adult, and I have the right to live a full life such as you and generations before us have. I will not accept nuclear war ever. You have a responsibility to listen to me and understand that I want to live.
Canada right now, I understand, does not have nuclear weapons on its soil. This is step in the right direction, but why are we supporting the Americans for their nuclear weapons, and allowing them to fly the cruise missile over Canada?
That is from a student in my riding.

It is just one more of those incompetent decisions of Canada Post. Mr. Speaker, do you remember the super-automated sorting plants that were supposed to help us get our mail the next day? Mr. Speaker, magazines owned and controlled by Canadians, unlike regional and local newspapers, are primarily a national as opposed to a local medium. Their focus is from a Canadian perspective. They entertain, educate, stimulate, record heritage, and express Canadian national identity. Postal subsidies for Canadian magazines have been in place for more than 70 years. The retention of special postal rates for magazines has been supported by the O'Leary Commission, the Davey special committee, and the Applebaum-Hebert Commission.
A 1984 study done for the Department of Communications emphasized the importance of concessionary postal rates. The report warned that, if it were decided to end the subsidy, the amount and rate of increase necessary to do so would likely threaten the survival of the Canadian industry.
The vitality of a strong domestic periodical industry is important to Canadian producers of goods and services. They reach, in a cost-effective way through advertising, Canadian consumers. The postal subsidy program is key to publishers, to advertisers, the Canadian economy. It should not be phased out.

Mr. Speaker, over the next four years the Brandon Research Station will receive over $164,000 from the federal Government to finance the search for a vaccine to control swine pneumonia. This disease is becoming more and more of a problem for hog producers all
across Canada. An effective vaccine will save producers a considerable amount of money.
The people who do agricultural research in Canada are the unsung heroes of the agricultural sector. Projects such as the one I have just mentioned may not sound many glamorous to Members of the House and they do not make very headlines, but researchers help our producers become more efficient. All of their work helps make Canada more competitive in the international market-place.
On behalf of the House I would like to commend all of those involved in agricultural research in Canada, and the federal Government for its continued commitment to this sector.

He said: Mr. Speaker, Motion No. 1, which refers to Clause 2, provides for a total removal of the current $3,500 limit on deductible contributions to pension plans, thus executives and other high income earners who now have to pay a portion of their pension contributions out of tax paid income will be able to benefit from a very rich deduction. Generally the people who benefit will be those with very high incomes and who therefore have a high marginal rate.
It is perhaps not normal to speak of these things, but the other day, at the instigation of the Government, Members of Parliament agreed to forego $1,000 of their income allegedly as a means to help to overcome the deficit. However, Clause 2 of the Bill will allow Members of Parliament who currently contribute about $5,500 per annum to their pension plan to take an additional deduction. The additional deduction will be in the order of some $2,000 a year, and I am speaking in round figures, and the consequence will be that Members of Parliament, if they are at a 50 per cent marginal rate, will have a tax saving of $1,000 because of this particular provision. That will go on in perpetuity, whereas the $1,000 cut they are taking in their salaries will come out of income before tax and, therefore, the cost to them is about $500 in terms of taxed income. I find this bizarre.
Of course, this is not just a matter for Members of Parliament, although I think there is a certain contradiction there, but is a matter which touches on all high income Canadians. The Government may say this clause and the clause relating to RRSPs is something which is desirable because it wants to encourage savings. I do not know if people want to necessarily discourage savings. The fact is that if people would spend a bit more in the country right now we might have a few more people back at work.
Motion No. 16 deals with Clause 57 of the Bill. Clause 57 raises the limit of contributions to an RRSP, a Registered Retirement Savings Plan, from the current $5,500 to $7,500 and the Government intends ultimately to raise this to $15,000. Once again this is a concession directed to middle and
Income Tax Act
upper income earners because 80 per cent or more of Canadians do not contribute to RRSPs and it is estimated that only 17 per cent or 18 per cent are in a position where they can contribute. Of those Canadians who contribute to RRSPs, a very large number currently do not have the resources to put in $5,500, let alone $7,500 or $15,000. Moreover, the contributions are going to come as a deduction from taxable income and there will be a limit on the proportion of one's income one can put into RRSPs. Once we get to the ultimate of $15,000, one will need an income of around $80,000 a year, I believe, in order to be able to take advantage of the full deductibility.
Let us look at that in terms of the tax expenditures involved. If someone puts aside $15,000 a year, and that is a deduction, and if they are at the top marginal rate, that means that other taxpayers will have to come up with $7,500 to make up for that person's tax saving because of this particular exemption, once it reaches the full limit announced by the Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson). This is not just a single kind of tax saving. If one puts $15,000 into an RRSP, one then receives the income on that RRSP, tax free, year after year after year until such time as the funds are withdrawn or begin to be used as retirement income. If one receives $1,500 a year on the income from the money one puts in and $15,000 has been put in, that means a tax saving for someone at the top marginal rate of $750 a year, again not in perpetuity but over five, 10 or maybe 25 years in which they will benefit from that particular tax saving. Frankly, I think that is too much.
I believe we are being unjust and unfair to ordinary Canadians when we ask them to pay through the nose for tax savings which in these two motions are being directed to upper income Canadians, whether they are contributing to pension plans or RRSPs. In addition, I would draw to the attention of the House the report of the select Committee on Pensions. That committee of the House of Commons strongly proposed that deductions for pension contributions, and presumably for RRSPs as well, should be in the form of a tax credit. However, that particular proposal has been ignored by the Government. That means that someone earning $20,000 a year who puts a few dollars aside into a pension plan or an RRSP will receive the equivalent of perhaps 20 per cent or 25 per cent of that money back because of the tax saving, because that is all their marginal rate is and all the deduction is worth to them, whereas someone at the top will receive far more. That seems to me to be unfair.
I would like to ask the Minister if he can respond to these points and tell us whether the Government would now be prepared to reconsider these clauses, particularly in light of our tax reform where we are trying to broaden the base and lower the rates. Here we are narrowing the base and, therefore, inevitably increasing the rates again on ordinary Canadians.

Mr. Speaker, that being said, I would like to comment on the two motions before the House today, and I would be tempted to think along the same philosophical lines as the Member who just spoke.
I have said repeatedly here in the House and in committee that as far as pensions and deductions for Registered Retirement Savings Plans are concerned, it would be far more useful to use tax credits instead of the present deductions because with tax credits, all taxpayers are given the same tax treatment, whether they are rich or poor, whether they can save a lot or just a little. The benefit would be the same and would not be more than the tax credit allowed. This would of course be in line with what the Minister of Finance indicated last July, when he referred to the Government's intention to follow the example of the United States with their tax reform. The U.S. tax reform is very limited in its application and applies only to middle- and low-income taxpayers. Under the new measure they may set aside certain sums of money, tax free, for their retirement plan, what we in Canada call Registered Retirement Savings Plans.
However, we are not considering a Bill on tax reform. We are merely considering the proposals made in the February 1986 Budget. It is rather unfortunate that the Bill comes at the end of a session. It was introduced in the House only a few weeks ago. In any case, it is not a Bill on tax reform. These are just a number of amendments which will be temporary, I imagine, until the Government finally decides to introduce more comprehensive tax reform measures.
If we were to accept the motions presented by the Hon. Member for Ottawa Centre (Mr. Cassidy), which are now before the House, I must say that, although I tend to agree with his philosophy, this would create an imbalance in the present Income Tax Act, because it would be necessary to adopt amendments that would be consequential on a number of other Acts, and I do not see how we could do so at this time.
Are we supposed to stop and greet people as they come in, Mr. Speaker? I'm not sure I approve, but let it pass, Christmas is almost here, and perhaps now we can get on with some serious debate.
Mr. Speaker, since the amendments proposed in Motions nos. 1 and 16 would throw the Tax Act off balance since there would only be two or three retirement plan provisions that would be concerned with income tax credits while the remainder would be dealing with exemptions, I feel this would not be very consistent. This is why, even though I agree with the idea
behind the proposal in Motions nos. 1 and 16, I am going to suggest to my colleagues that they oppose it for technical reasons, for reasons of consistency with the whole of the Tax Act. Under a more general tax reform, however, I think it would be appropriate to examine closely the suggestions contained in those two motions that I did introduce during discussion in committee.

Mr. Speaker, we have proposed these amendments to introduce some fairness into the tax system. It is not that we want to discourage saving. In fact, we want to encourage those who cannot participate in company pension plans, such as professionals and small business people, to save. But this is surely a question of fairness.
The proposals made by the Government, both in Bill C-23 and in later announcements by the Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson), will allow the more well-to-do individuals in our society to deduct up to $15,000 per year as a result of RRSP contributions. It does not take too many brains to figure out that those in the higher income levels will benefit more than those in the lower and middle income levels. In fact, those in lower income levels will be further restricted by the amount of contribution they can make to an RRSP. That is because the legislation provides that only a certain percentage of taxable income can be contributed to an RRSP. For middle and low income Canadians as opposed to those in higher income brackets this means a smaller contribution.
Let us consider someone with $20,000 in taxable income. That person is in the 20 per cent to 30 per cent income tax range. Thus, in essence, their contribution is matched through the tax system at around 20 per cent to 30 per cent. A person who is in the 50 per cent income tax bracket has one-half of the contribution paid for by the Government through the tax system because of the decreased tax that individual will have to pay.
Thus we Find ourselves in a situation in which wealthy Canadians are able to have one-half of their pension plans paid for by the public because of tax savings. Low income Canadians will not have that same opportunity. They will find that only 20 per cent of their pension will be paid for by the public through the tax system. This is a basic and glaring unfairness. It tilts the system to the benefit of the wealthy at the expense of the poor.
What we are proposing is not a radical, new proposal at all. It is a proposal that has been made by a standing committee of the House of Commons which considered the matter of pensions and which recommended that a certain amount of deductions be no longer allowed as tax deductions per se but as tax credits. This would provide a fairness to the system so that a person with $20,000 in taxable income would have the same effective tax reduction because of his RRSP contributions as an individual who is in the $50,000, $75,000 or $100,000 taxable income range. What we are doing through these
December 16, 1986

amendments is trying to introduce an important measure of fairness into the tax system.
The Government and the Minister of Finance, in several of his speeches, have made a strong commitment to tax reform. We welcome everything he has said in this regard so far. He seems to be giving us an indication that he is serious about tax reform. He seems to be saying that it will not just be windowdressing and that, indeed, he will make a serious attempt to rewrite the basic tax structure and operations of the country so that we will have greater fairness.
This is the opportunity for creating fairness in the system and for correcting an unfairness that now exists. I urge Hon. Members to accept our amendments.

He said: Perhaps the Minister could comment on this particular case. This is the rather curious business where the Government has decided that the various granting councils should go out and set up their stands and try to find funds from outside in order to raise the increased funding, rather than have it come from Government.
The problem which the committee addressed directly is the fact that there is prejudicial treatment given to one of these three granting councils. As Members know, the three councils are the Natural Sciences and Engineering Research Council, the Medical Research Council, and the Social Sciences and Humanities Research Council.
As the Budget Papers indicated, beginning in 1987-88 the Government intends to match dollar for dollar increased private sector contributions received by the granting councils to a certain annual maximum increase.

A consequential income tax change will be made to ensure that the private sector participant will be entitled to research and development tax treatment for his contribution-

Other contributions to such councils will be treated as gifts to Her Majesty and as such will be deductible in computing the donor's taxable income.
That means that certain types of contributions to the Natural Sciences Council and the Medical Research Council will be treated as R and D expense and, therefore, will get

favoured status, whereas in general no contributions that were gathered in this way by the Social Sciences and Humanities Research Council will receive that favoured status at all. The Finance Committee found itself in a difficult situation because Members from all sides felt that there was injustice and prejudicial treatment with respect to the Social Sciences and Humanities Research Council.
I have met people in the social sciences and know the degree to which a great deal of academic excellence in this country hangs on the work and the funding of that particular council, and the degree to which there is a dearth of other funding alternatives for areas like the humanities, the social sciences, and many areas such as psychology and sociology which are extremely important in terms of understanding where we are going as a country. that it had lost all meaning. We would be in great trouble defining what it meant at all. Mr. Speaker, I sympathize with the difficulty that the Secretary of State for Finance (Mr. Hockin) has mentioned in terms of defining research and development to include the social sciences and humanities, but not to open it up in such a way as to allow all manner of abuses to occur.
My mind then goes to the next situation where he illustrates the difficulty of conducting social and economic policies through the tax system. In part, that is what tax reform is all about. The tax system should stop being used for social, economic and scientific purposes and programs. There is a certain ring of regional discrimination.
I will simply speak as a westerner, but I could make the same case if I came from another region of Canada other than central Canada. If we are looking for research and development to take place through the private sector, presumably decisions will be made by supporting firms which tend to have their head offices in central Canada and tend to be concentrated geographically there. If we are looking at matching funds from the corporate sector for research or at research being tied through the private sector, it will have a natural bias toward being focused in central Canada as opposed to the regions.
It is not a major issue. I do not want to suggest it is. I do not want to suggest either that it will be a major effort toward discrimination or that there is any intentional discrimination. However, inadvertently and because of the reality of Canada and its industrial heartland or where the private sector tends to be headquartered, it would result in a certain bias in research being done in such a way that it would discriminate against the far West. Would the Minister agree with those comments?

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Is there unanimous consent to allow the Minister to make a short reply?
Agreed.

Mr. Speaker, that is an interesting question. It is true in the world today, in terms of research, that we often cannot produce world-class research without a critical mass of researchers. Very often this means, when we talk about the research side, that much research is concentrated in certain places. For example, medical research clearly has certain homes in Canada. I quite agree that it is not widely distributed across the country. However, that is sort of the nature of research.
I remind the Hon. Member of the nature of the private sector. Let us take western institutions, for example, in the interior of British Columbia or in the Canadian Prairies.
Income Tax Act
Saskatoon has a very interesting and critical mass of space research. The co-operatives and other parts of the private sector are strong and important in certain parts of British Columbia and Alberta. We also have the oil and gas industry, potash, and so on. Perhaps researchers have not gone to these people and said: "We can do some research of use to you to strengthen your infrastructure". Maybe this would encourage them to do it, and that is why I support it. When it comes out in the wash, it could be that it is not totally balanced. That is the point of the Hon. Member. Perhaps it is a reason for us to examine it carefully in the future and see how it evolves.

Mr. Speaker, the motion now under discussion in fact has to do with agencies in the social field, the so-called political and social sciences, which have a hard time getting funds that should come from businesses because donations for funding their research and development work could hardly be viewed as connected with the operations of the firm making such donations.
In other words, the reason for this debate is, taking the example of any type of business, let us say a bank for instance, a large Canadian bank that would like to support the Faculty of Social Sciences at the University of Toronto by making a major donation to research and development. In order for the Royal Bank to consider that as funding for research and development, it would have to prove that the research done by the University of Toronto's Faculty of Social Sciences can help the operations of the donor or of the person who wants to invest in the research and development field. This is extremely difficult.
This is why all university groups, universities and departments that are involved in research in the area of economic and social sciences, in a political and social sense, have a hard time getting their research projects funded. The goal is therefore to ask the Government to find the appropriate formula.
In his answers, the Minister stated earlier that if we open up the definition, because in my view we could solve the problem by way of regulations rather than by way of the legislation itself.
For the reasons mentioned I am prepared to accept clause 6 as it is, but we create a problem in the sense that it will be even more difficult to finance research in economic and social sciences departments.
In response to one of my colleagues the Minister said a moment ago that it might become extremely difficult to establish the criteria concerning the limits of the tax field which the Government is prepared to abandon for this kind of research and development.
Mr. Speaker, I would suggest that the Minister exaggerates to a certain extent because companies do not actually go out of their way to hand out millions of dollars just to get a tax exemption worth many hundred dollars. Indeed there are

December 16, 1986
Income Tax Act
operating costs and, to my mind, these would act as a natural check likely to prevent some of the abuses the Minister mentioned.
All things considered and given the field of activities which make it more difficult to come up with an acceptable definition, I think we might have at Government level-either the Department of the Secretary of State which looks after higher post-secondary education grants, or the Department of Finance, or other Government sectors-a committee or an assessment board which would rule and authorize donations as being directly or indirectly related to the operations of a company prepared to invest in research and development.
I would think we can find a way to devise a solution without necessarily resorting to legislation. Perhaps the Minister might consider the matter and amend the regulations, or even the legislation if it comes to that. Still I think there is a way to overcome this difficulty.
I remind the Minister that we have received strong representations from university circles, and I suspect he did too. As I see it, the problem is serious enough to be worthy of his consideration.
Having said this, Mr. Speaker, I do not see how I can support Motion No. 2 because by doing so I might be making it easier still for tax evaders in the field of research and development.
This is why I will vote against the motion now before the House because it will not achieve the basic objective. Still I urge the Minister to consider very carefully every opportunity there might be to solve the problem of research in the field of social affairs without actually incurring huge tax losses, at least no higher than the tax expenditures related to clause 6 as it is now drafted.
