speakeroldname: Mr. Simon de Jong (Regina East) (for Mr. Cassidy) moved:
speechtext:
Motion No. 3
That Bill C-23, be amended by deleting Clause 12.

Motion No. 6
That Bill C-23, be amended by deleting Clause 35.
He said: Mr. Speaker, I am sorry for being late. The difficulty is in trying to be in the committee and elsewhere at the same time. This motion relates to the flow-through clauses. The Government announced in the Budget that its intention was to make use of these shares easier and, among other things, to remove the possibility of third party liability from individuals. Elsewhere certain rules relating to limited partnerships are being somewhat tightened, but in this case the use of flow-through shares is being eased.
Once again we get into the situation where there is effectively an enormous tax expenditure involved, and despite the fact that tax reform is on the horizon, the Government does not appear to have questioned whether it should now begin to tighten down in areas where it is being quite generous. The rules allow a 100 per cent write-off against taxable income of Canadian exploration expense, a 30 per cent per annum writeoff of Canadian development expense, and a 10 per cent per annum write-off of Canadian oil and gas property expense. That means that if the investment is made in the flow-through shares and if the corporation then renounces the deduction for its own purposes and passes it back or flows it through back to the investor, a wealthy Canadian tax filer whose marginal tax rate is in the 50 per cent bracket can then invest $10,000 in flow-through shares in a small mining or oil company and get an immediate write-off against taxable income for that whole amount if the company spends that amount on exploration within the tax year or within 12 months. The tax saved in this case would be about $5,000.
When we are talking about tax saving, we are talking about somebody else paying that amount. If that amount is not paid by the taxpayer, then we are all going to pay it, as we have been reminded on many occasions by the Government, through the means of an increased deficit and through paying interest over many years because of a concession such as in this case. Tax savings are only in the minds of the people who receive them, and those are normally wealthy Canadians. 1 do not think there are many people in my constituency who are in a position to sink $10,000 in an oil, gas or mining exploration with flow-through shares. There are a few. They live in certain parts of my riding. Some of them even vote for me, I guess, but most of the people in my riding do not have that kind of situation. Even if they did and were able to put $2,000 or $3,000 into one of these investments and gain certain benefits, the tax benefits they would receive are a lot less because this is a deduction from taxable income and, therefore, the higher the bracket, the more the people of Canada will be called upon to share in that particular investment.
The pages of The Globe and Mail and The Ottawa Citizen and business pages of other newspapers across the country are
December 16, 1986

jammed at this time of the year with various types of tax dodges and tax shelters. The Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson) at every Budget says: "We are doing away with MURBS, limited partnerships and with these means by which tax is avoided". Yet I picked up a paper last night and read that for a mere $1,000 or $2,000 I or somebody else could generate tax losses in the first year of $23,000. I do not know how it is done.
I almost admire the creativity of the people who devise these kinds of schemes at the same time as I deplore the twisted distorted priorities of a society where somebody who has a big tax bracket and $1,000 or $2,000 to put aside can get $23,000 in tax losses and save $11,000 or $12,000 in taxation in one year while at the same time there are hundreds if not thousands of people in my constituency who do not have enough food to get themselves to the end of the month every month. People are having to go to food banks and the food banks are running out of food. These banks cannot serve the needs. The Government sees that its priority is to put more products, as the financial industry calls them, into place to allow more wealthy Canadians to avoid tax. The Government will then turn around and tell us that we need a business transfer tax or we need a higher rate of taxation on ordinary Canadians in order to provide these tax loopholes, these legal tax avoidance mechanisms, such as the one contained in Clause 35.
When we were devising the amendments in this area we had a choice. We could have tried to change, amend and improve the various measures being put forward by the Government. I decided, and my colleagues accepted, that where you have a measure which should fundamentally be re-thought, which is far too broad for the declared purpose, which is to get some needed exploration expense and activity going in the northern parts of my province, that is, Quebec, the oil and gas areas and so on, rather than simply saying there is a bit of good here and there is a lot of bad, we should simply tell the Government to stop it, take the measure away, start all over again, and strike out the loopholes. Then, if the Government has to have targeted measures in the form of tax credits, grants or other means to encourage certain types of desirable activity, for goodness' sake let it do it that way, but let it not do it in the broad brush kind of way which is being proposed here.
This is a related subject. It will not be debated directly here, but I mention it briefly. The Government purports to have reduced the use of limited partnership with the clauses elsewhere in the Bill. I want to say to the Minister of Finance and his deputy that already the high priced help in Bay Street, in St. James Street and probably Wall Street as well, are now looking at means by which they can avoid that, even by taking advantage of the new provisions which are put into this Bill. If you provide loopholes, inevitably the loopholes will be used. We have to have a commitment which I am afraid I do not see yet from the Government. If it is really intent on tax reform, it should not fiddle around at the edges with something like this. The Government should not increase some pension deductibility and say, "Well that is just temporary". The Government should be serious about tax reform from now until the end of
Income Tax Act
the mandate in 1988 or 1989 and systematically ensure that every measure that affects the tax system is a strong step forward to tax reform rather than taking two steps forward and one a half backward, which is the record of the Government right now, or one and a half steps forward and two back.

Mr. Speaker, let me reply to the Hon. Member because his points were wide-ranging and I think it is important that I do reply. I think the Hon. Member knows that flowthrough shares and the tax arrangements for them are not designed for the riding of Ottawa Centre. They are designed, as the Member knows, for northern Ontario, northern Quebec, the Northwest Territories, the Yukon and northern Manitoba, Alberta and so on. As a matter of fact, it is the northern parts of our provinces that are the most neglected parts of our society economically and in every other sense. We must do something for those parts. That is what is behind the flowthrough shares.
I want to assure the Hon. Member that we cannot stand still while looking at tax reform. We have to govern. However, quite frankly, flow-through shares have been very effective in creating very meaningful economic activity in a neglected area of Canada. How do you do it except through private investment? The Hon. Member is asking Government to do this exploration. Government is not designed to be a risk taker. It is not designed to make the tough decisions about what risks should be taken. That naturally belongs to the private sector. If you are going to ask the private sector to invest, you have to ask those who have money to invest. This policy is not aimed at helping the wealthy of Ottawa centre. It is aimed at helping the people in northern Canada and making sure that risk decisions are not taken by Government but by the private sector.
The second point deals with limited partnerships and the deductibility of losses. That is part of the question of tax reform, but let me ask the Hon. Member this question. If someone incurs a large loss which cannot be written off in one year, should they be prohibited from writing it off over a couple of other years? What if a farmer, a logger or a small businessman is caught in some terrible catastrophe? What if they do not have enough income to write it off in one year? You should be able to write it off in other years as well, but the Hon. Member would remove that right with his amendment. Therefore I am very firm in my conviction that this motion should be defeated because it goes against the very heart of what we are trying to do.

Mr. Speaker, I have trouble understanding the reasoning behind the motions presented by the Members of the New Democratic Party. When the Liberal Government introduced these measures, as a stimulus to economic development in the mining areas of Quebec and Northern Ontario, the results were extremely positive.

December 16, 1986
Income Tax Act
Not long ago, I was visiting the Val d'Or area, where I met people who do research and development in the mining industry. I spent most of the afternoon talking to them to find out about the impact on the local economy of what are known as flow-through shares and what the positive impact had been of this tax remedy introduced by the Liberal Government at the beginning of the eighties or around the middle of the seventies. I asked whether they felt it had made a positive contribution.
I must say, Mr. Speaker, that the economic activity generated by this tax provision has had a considerable impact. This is true in Northern Quebec but it also applies to the mining industry in Ontario and to the mining, gas and petroleum industry across this country. The results have been particulary positive for people who are prospecting for gold, because the price of gold and the extremely high cost of research and exploration.
In Northern Quebec, this tax provision, which became more widespread over the years as taxpayers realized the kind of benefits it could bring and also as mining companies realized how they could finance certain activities related to the development of their resources-this provision has had a considerable economic impact.
When I met with the mining prospectors, I was told about certain economic impact studies. The prospectors claim that they can show, with the statistics to prove it, that the benefits of the tax concessions granted by the Government during the last few years to promote investment in the mining sector have greatly exceeded the cost of these measures for the state.
This is why I find it hard to understand how the Hon. Member of the New Democratic Party can claim that these measures are only designed to help people with high incomes.
Mr. Speaker, these tax provisions deal with situations where there is a risk. If you purchase flow-through shares and the prospecting company finds nothing and cannot find any mineral whatsoever, this will mean a total loss and the investor will lose his money. There is therefore a risk and it is because this risk is great that it is compensated by tax benefits. I do not understand why the New Democratic Party attacks remote regions such as the Abitibi and Northern Ontario, which need practical support to develop their economy. I can assure you that, in those regions, if flow-through shares were completely eliminated tomorrow, it would mean the loss of thousands of jobs created because of the tax benefits brought in by the Liberal Government a few years ago and maintained by this Bill.
1 also find it hard to understand the attitude of the NDP in wanting to remove these two sections. This goes against their own arguments as the purpose of these provisions is to close the loopholes and better define how these tax benefits will apply so that there will be less danger of abuse. The members of the NPD are fully entitled to disagree about the objectives we were trying to meet a few years ago by bringing in flowthrough shares to help mining prospection, but they will
certainly not meet their objectives if the two motions before us are passed. On the contrary, it would make it completely impossible to apply the law because we would be removing two provisions which are at the centre of the legislation. This is why, since flow-through shares have contributed a lot to the development of Northern Quebec, Northern Ontario and other mining regions in Canada and since the two motions now under consideration would make it virtually impossible to apply our tax laws, I shall have to vote against these motions.

Mr. Speaker, I find it shocking-I guess that is the only expression to use- that the NDP would try to eliminate something that has done so much for so many Canadians. Why eliminate something that has developed so many jobs over the last number of years and has brought so much to the economy of the northern part of Canada? The members of the NDP have always said they fight for the little guy. I must say this proves they do not. They are more interested in making political points in the House of Commons than in looking after the people who send us here to do a job for them. This just shows they are more interested in Bay Street than they are in the grass roots. I find it deplorable that the Hon. Member, a former Leader of the NDP in Ontario, would not reflect on what he knows has benefited northern Ontario for many years.
I urge Members to continue with what has been beneficial to each and every one of us over the last number of years. Flowthrough shares have helped develop many small businesses, whether it be the corner grocery store, a diamond driller, prospector-developer, or junior mining company. There is only one way to get the needed investment and that is through flowthrough shares. I do not think that since I have been elected I have had more correspondence on any other subject than I have had from people who were concerned that we were going to remove the concept of flow-through shares. I hope each Member of the House rejects this outrageous proposal put forward by the Hon. Member for Ottawa Centre (Mr. Cassidy).

Mr. Speaker, I wish to join with my colleagues the Hon. Member for Timiskaming (Mr. MacDougall) and the Hon. Member for Laval-des-Rapides (Mr. Garneau) concerning this amendment as well as the flowthrough shares. And as I stated in the House on November 19, I was telling representatives of the Canada mining industry that our prospectors in Abitibi-Temiscamingue, in Chapais and Chibougamau were firmly demanding both the Canada and Quebec Governments to maintain the flow-through share system in the mining exploration industry. I have been fighting for several months for the Government to maintain this program, because it is important for the Northern Quebec area and all the other areas in Canada-and when I say all the other regions of Canada, I mean Northern British Columbia as
*
December 16, 1986

well as Nothern Ontario, both great regions, as well as Saskatchewan, the whole North and especially the great mining areas represented by Hon. Members. I must tell Members of the New Democratic Party who are trying to do away with benefits in those large regions, that in those regions we have no Star War spinoffs, no F-18 spinoffs, no spinoffs from shipbuilding for the Government of Canada. The only spinoffs we have in those regions-the Abitibi, Temiscamingue and all the other regions in Canada, especially in the North- come from mining exploration-flow-through shares have been an efficient incentive in many of those regions. We are aware of the current renewal, especially in Quebec, and recently the Quebec Association of Prospectors produced a $100,000 study that was funded both by prospectors and the Quebec Government, an economic impact study on mining exploration funding through flow-through shares and limited partnerships.
1 can tell you that in that report-but let me quote a few examples, a few lines from it. The study on various flowthrough provisions used in Quebec deals covers the period from 1980, starting date for the Quebec Government, through 1985. Some $315 million had been invested by 1985 by Quebec taxpayers over that period. An examination of each public issue floated produced data on the amounts that went to fund exploration in Quebec. The latter total was figured out by the study team to be $269 million. On the other hand, during 1984-85, a total amount of $61 million was gathered all across Canada and outside Quebec, and may I repeat outside Quebec, that is in Canada and in that province, for a total of $330 million. The Quebec tax cost is based on $315 million invested by Quebecers, while economic spinoffs and the federal tax cost were based on $330 million in 1985 spent in Quebec.
If I may go on, Mr. Speaker, in view of that preamble, the tax cost for both levels of Government is estimated at $239.5 million in 1985, that is $104.25 million for the federal Government and $135.2 million for the provincial Government. The program's financial and tax spinoffs are expressed under two different headings-first, spinoffs from exploration expenditures themselves, both direct, indirect and induced, and second spinoffs from mineral discoveries, their development and future mining operations. It is obvious that this last measure basically remains in the assessment of the program, because the entire program is aimed at improving on the mineral reserves in Quebec generally and in Canada as a whole.
As I said, with respect to the flow-through shares, either in Northern Ontario or in the Temiscamingue area, either in Northern Saskatchewan or throughout the provinces, the message is as follows: Even as far as our Minister of Finance is concerned, the flow-through shares should be kept at 133 1/3. And we know that as recently as last week, the Quebec Government has maintained some flow-through shares at 133 1/3. They are at the same rate as at the federal level.
Before concluding, Mr. Speaker, I should like to mention some discoveries that were developed in Quebec.
Income Tax Act
The 8 discoveries retained for financial and fiscal purposes will require during the forthcoming two years investments of about $300 million for their development and they will yield a production worth $2 billion during a 10-year period. We may be sure that some of those discoveries will yield revenues beyond that 10-year period, but the task force has found it advisable to be more conservative and to set that 10-year period.
Moreover, we have figured out in 1985 dollars the entire future economic impact so that after 10 years, the actual value of a $1 dollar investment is next to negligible.
Mr. Speaker, I agree with my colleagues the two previous speakers who dealt with flow-through shares, that is the Hon. Member for Laval-des-Rapides (Mr. Garneau) and the Hon. Member for Timiskaming (Mr. MacDougall). Flow-through shares are important for large areas.
I know that many Members in this House represent urban areas but I also know that if the Hon. Member for Laval-des-Rapides comes from an urban area he is more concerned about larger remote areas.
Mr. Speaker, I will vote against that motion.

Mr. Speaker, I would like to clarify a few things. The Hon. Member for Timiskaming (Mr. MacDougall) stood up and huffed and puffed himself into great indignation. In no way are we suggesting that the mining and exploration operations in the northern regions are essential. In no way are we suggesting that the flow-through provisions have not been of significant assistance.
I rise on a point of order Mr. Speaker.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Order. The Hon. Member for Abitibi (Mr. St. Julien) rises on a point of order.
Mr. Speaker, while I was concluding my comments a while ago, perhaps it was as a result of my deep feeling for my Abitibi constituency, but I should like to say that I am against the motion.

If I may continue, Mr. Speaker, we are not questioning how the flow-through provision has been helpful. In fact, when the NDP task force, of which I was a member, toured the country we asked a pretty standard question of witnesses across the country. We asked them to give one example of a tax expenditure that was beneficial. The only example we were given was the flow-through provision, and we heard that in various parts of the country.
We are flagging this for the attention of the House in order to begin the debate on tax reform. If memory serves me right, the Department said that it cost Canadian taxpayers $450 million for this particular item. In other words, there are $450 million in uncollected taxes because certain individuals and

December 16, 1986
Income Tax Act
investors availed themselves of this opportunity. I am not saying that that is a bad investment. Perhaps it is a good investment. Perhaps we will indeed get out of it $450 million plus economic activity. I think it is worth considering.
Surely if we are going to study a tax reform proposal we will have to consider this provision as well and ask whether the public is getting $450 million worth of benefits from it. Can the benefits of this provision be delivered in another way? These are questions which the Finance Committee, the Government, the Department of Finance and this Flouse will have to ask. That is the type of debate we are hoping to initiate here and now through our amendment. We are not questioning the benefits of the flow-through provision as they have occurred. Let me repeat that we are attempting to begin the discussion to determine whether we did receive $450 million worth of benefits. My request is no different from what the Minister of State for Finance stated in his comments earlier when debating this amendment. He admitted that if we are going to go through tax reform we will also have to ask these questions about the flow-through shares. The Government must admit that this item will also have to be scrutinized within a tax reform regime.
We must consider whether there is another way in which these benefits can occur to northern mining and exploration without necessarily costing the taxpayers $450 million. Is there another way to engender greater public accountability and scrutiny?
We must remember that this is an inducement in which the public takes half the risk. Those in the 50 per cent tax bracket who risk $100,000 or $10,000 on an investment will receive 50 per cent of it back on their taxes. In other words, the public is subsidizing those economic activities by 50 per cent, depending on the taxpayer.
There are Hon. Members, particularly those in the Conservative Party, who believe in the free enterprise system. They believe that those who take risks and are successful should not be taxed to death but allowed to accumulate wealth that way. If their investment fails, they should also face the consequences. However, it is not quite so simple because according to this provision, half of the risk is covered by the taxpayer, which undermines that philosophy of risk taking. Since half the risk is covered by taxpayers, we are interested in a little more public accountability in this area.
I am somewhat disappointed by the reaction of Conservative Members who enjoy taking political potshots at this amendment.

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
speechtext: At your inconsistencies.

I remind the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Epp) that within six months his Government will have to ask these same questions and enter into very much the same debate if tax reform is going to be a serious exercise. I
invite those Hon. Members to join in some serious debate now, or look like fools in six months when they will have to address these questions at that stage. If those Members and the Minister had any understanding of tax reform, they would not be ridiculing this debate.

speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
speechtext: It is a ridiculous discussion.

It is a discussion that will take place if there is to be a serious exercise in tax reform. We will have to ask some difficult questions about our tax system, some of which may not be politically advantageous. We will have to consider seriously some of the "holy cows" in our tax system. In order to have a serious tax reform exercise in this country, we must be able occasionally to ask some politically difficult questions. That is what we are attempting in this amendment, and I am disappointed that government Members in particular have not seen fit to enter into this debate and seriously discuss the issues involved. Rather, they have been more concerned about making some cheap political points. I suggest that if there is a serious debate about tax reform in six months, those Members will be embarrassed because the questions we are raising today will be the ones raised by the Department of Finance and the Finance Committee.

Mr. Speaker, my, how they slither and squirm over there in the New Democratic Party. We saw the spectacle of the Hon. Member for Ottawa Centre (Mr. Cassidy), a gentleman who has never seen more than two blocks from the city centre, get up to say that we must get rid of flow-through shares. They do not care what effect it will have on Abitibi, Timiskaming, northern Quebec or elsewhere.
The Hon. Member for Regina West (Mr. de Jong), however, does know a little-I stress "little"-so he is trying to back down from that position, saying that they did not really mean it but were just flagging the question for future debate.
The people of Canada and those who rely on the exploration and development industry for their jobs know what would happen if we had a New Democratic Government. They know what would happen to their jobs if, God forbid, that ever happened. They will take the right precautionary measures at the next election to make sure that it never happens.
I will not dwell at length on this because my colleagues have already stressed the importance of the flow-through shares to the minerals industry.
Mineral exploration is very susceptible to taxation. One only need consider what happened in the late 1960s when the Liberals began imposing capital gains tax on the prospectors' once-in-a-lifetime find. That brought about a decline in mineral exploration. Fortunately, the Liberals saw the errors of their ways and, while they cannot go back to correct the situation, they did introduce flow-through shares. That is what this Government is continuing. It helped to mobilize those funds again in mineral exploration, providing many jobs and
December 16, 1986

many opportunities in parts of the country like that which 1 represent.
In my opinion, in the present state of affairs, taking into account the low value of many mineral commodities, it would be disastrous if the flow-through shares were to be taken off, as advocated by the NDP. Therefore, I am in complete support of the Minister of State for Finance (Mr. Hockin) and those of my colleagues who have spoken on this subject. We want to maintain the status quo with respect to flow-through shares, at least for the forseeable future.

I was saying, Mr. Speaker, that it is evolutionary in that much of what is incorporated in this Bill was already incorporated into previous remission orders made under the Financial Administration Act.
I have been involved in this matter for many years as have many other Hon. Members on this side of the House. The former Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development, the present Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Epp), has been very active in this area. The Minister of State for Science and Technology (Mr. Oberle) has been very instrumental over the years in having this Bill brought in.
This measure finds considerable support in the northern region because it is something they have wanted for a long time. In particular, the union movements, the NWT Federation, the Yukon Federation of Labour, the Steel Workers Union, the Teachers Association and Public Service Unions have always been very active in support. I Find it very difficult to understand why the New Democratic Party has gone against the wishes of the labour movement. In fact, it was the Canadian Labour Congress which was very instrumental in putting pressure on the Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson) to make these necessary changes. Therefore, why on earth would the NDP go against its supposed friends in the Canadian Labour Congress?
I want to offer some congratulations to all the many people, whether they be in the labour movement, the territorial or municipal Governments or in the private sector, who have worked so hard to make this day possible. Those are my comments on Motion No. 5 moved by the New Democratic Party.
I would now like to be specific about Motion No. 4, moved by myself, which deals with Section 110.7(d) of the Income Tax Act as it will be after this Bill is passed. The motion is in respect of the travel deduction. The new Section 110.7 (d)
states:
In computing the taxable income-there may be deducted
(d) an amount received, or the value of a benefit received or enjoyed, in the
year by him in respect of his employment in the area by a person with whom
he was dealing at arm's length in respect of travelling expenses incurred by
him, to the extent that-
The effect of my amendment would be to remove the words "-by a person with whom he was dealing at arm's length-".
If we leave that in, it creates a great difference between employees of Government-of which there are many in the North because it is the greatest industry in the North, unfortunately-those employees of major concerns, say, mining companies, and small businesses and their employees, on the other hand.
Small businesses have always been at a disadvantage, especially in the North, as they try to compete for employment services. They have had to compete with wealthy Governments and corporations to get good employees. In the case of a small company, a painting outfit, for example, one very often finds that one of the employees in a three-person outfit might be the brother-in-law of the proprietor and the third person might be someone off the street, so to speak. The way this section is worded, the employee off the street would be able to take advantage of the new amendments to the Income Tax Act but the proprietor's brother-in-law would not. That does not really make too much sense. I have received quite a bit of correspondence on this issue, especially from the Yukon. I would like to quote a few paragraphs out of a letter I received from Designers North Ltd. of Whitehorse, Yukon, which explains the necessity for the amendment I have introduced probably better than I could myself. It reads:
The proposed provision has been drawn to preclude a deduction for such travel expenses where the individual is not dealing at "arm's length" with the person providing the benefit. Thus, sole proprietors, partners in partnerships, employees of companies they control and employees of any of the foregoing who are related-within the meaning of Section 251 of the Income Tax Act-to such sole proprietors, such partners or the controlling individual or controlling group of such companies are not allowed this deduction.
In meeting with the Yukon Committee for Fairness in the Taxation of Northern Equity Payments (the "Committee") your Department indicated that "self employed" persons would not be entitled to this deduction. As a result, the Committee was operating under the perception that the deduction would only not be available for sole proprietors and partners in partnerships and only until such time as these persons incorporated. As the foregoing indicates, such is not the case. Incorporated or not, this deduction would not be available. "Self employed" is thus an incorrect term to be used in describing who would not be entitled to this deduction.
And what is the justification for discriminating against small businessses and small business people in this manner? In the meeting referred to above, your Department purported to justify this exception on the basis that "self-employed" persons could expense such travel. This justification does not hold water. No business or businessperson can expense non-business related travel for himself or herself much less for his or her family. The type of travel that is involved here is, by definition, not business travel.
In allowing such a deduction your Government is recognizing that people who live in the north or other isolated areas have higher travel expenses and require a tax subsidy in that regard. It also reflects your Government's policy to encourage development of the north. This reasoning is equally applicable to small business and small business people.
Nor, with the limits on the cost of such travel and the number of trips allowable in any one year, can this deduction be abused by small businesses or small business people. There is little doubt that it is not your Government's intention to limit this deduction in this manner.
There are a couple of other points I wish to place on the record. In my reading of what we have before us, the travel allowance would also apply to family members of the taxpayer and not necessarily to the taxpayer himself. My interpretation
December 16, 1986

of a phrase such as "travelling expenses incurred by him" is that if my wife were to travel and I were to pay for her ticket, then that would be a travel expense incurred by me as a taxpayer. If the Minister of State for Finance (Mr. Hockin) has an opportunity to speak on this matter, then I would, of course, like his confirmation that that is indeed the fact and that family members of taxpayers can take advantage of these proposed provisions.
Another comment I have to make relates to intra-territorial travel. Prior to this advantages were given only to people who travelled from the remote areas of the North to a southern location. It is now my interpretation that people who travel within the Territories can take advantage of the new provisions.
I see that my time has expired, Mr. Speaker. Thank you very much indeed.

Mr. Speaker, I have several points I wish to make on this subject. I have met with the Committee for Tax Fairness, which is a broadly representative group, and we talked about this issue about nine or ten months ago during the course of our tax probe tour. The rules of the House make it a bit difficult to bring a matter to the attention of the House where it is appropriate at the report stage of a Bill. Had I known that the Hon. Member for Western Arctic (Mr. Nickerson) would raise his amendment, then that would have allowed me to make the points I will now make.
What I have to say may sound somewhat curious. However, since Motion No. 5 is to be voted on separately, and I have raised a point with you about that, Mr. Speaker, then I ask Hon. Members to join with us in voting against it. The motion is for the deletion of Clause 34. Therefore I support the clause as it stands even though I have substantial reservations about it, which I will now express.
I wish to pay some credit to Members from northern Canada who have worked hard to bring about the recognition that this is a substantial improvement on what now exists. As I understand it, if an employer provides subsidized or free housing, or air trips, they do not enter into taxable income and are therefore essentially tax-exempt. However, an individual who is running a small business or who works for a small business, for example, native people, do not generally benefit from the same tax provisions. Therefore it is inequitable and biased, to some extent, toward people from southern Canada and against native northerners or people who have sunk their roots into northern Canada and who have no intention or desire to move back south. So in that sense this measure is positive.
The problem with it is that it benefits more those with higher incomes. That is the major point I wished to raise. As I have said, we will not oppose the passage of this Bill although the clause is included in it. We will ask Members not to support the motion to delete Clause 34.
Income Tax Act
I have done some calculations which show that a married employee with a $20,000 income living in Whitehorse, Yellowknife or some other northern community receives a tax savings of about $1,000. That employee's supervisor, or the general manager of a large company in the North, who has an income in the $50,000 range will receive a concession that is valued at about $2,700. I believe that this is inequitable, particularly given the living costs in northern Canada, with which the Hon. Member for Western Arctic is well familiar. The worker with the modest income who has a tough time meeting the costs of housing, food, clothing and of other goods and services receives a deduction which is worth about 40 per cent of the deduction that is given someone earning two and a half times as much. In other words, the measure works backward. If anything, I think that the concession should work in the other direction. I recognize that for people who are not organized, and for native people, this is an important step forward. I point out as well that because a tax credit is not used for the employee on a modest income who wishes to fly out of the North with his or her spouse on one occasion, perhaps at Christmas to spend time with family or to take a holiday in some warmer part of the world, the cost of the trip is only subsidized in terms of tax savings to the tune of about 15 per cent. The tax cost of the trip for the high income employee is subsidized to a greater extent. The high income employee, if he does not have air travel arrangements as part of his contract, is better able to pay for tickets and take trips than an employee who receives a modest income and who may not be able to cough up the money in the first place to get out of northern Canada even one or two times every year.
The final point I wish to raise is one which I believe is being addressed by the Department of Finance. I wish to put it on the record now because it was clearly a concern of people in Yukon. My colleague from Yukon who is not here now, although I am sure he has made this point previously, suggests that in many communities in northern Canada there is no rental market. There is no way by which one can judge what the rental value of a particular house should be. If there is, it will be saying that such and such a residence cost $150,000 to construct and therefore the rent should be based on the capital value of the property. This yields very high values on imputed rent. I wish to suggest that this measure can be extremely unfair to northern people. I believe this matter is now being addressed by the Finance Department. However, to be fair, where there is not an active and representative local rental market, as may conceivably exist in places such as Yellowknife and Whitehorse-and I am not even sure about that-then I think we have to agree that where shelter is being provided as a part of a contract, then the imputed value of that shelter should not be put at such an extraordinary price that, effectively, the employee will have to pay tax on an imputed value well above the $450 per month deductible that is in place. I point out to the Minister that the $450 is in itself not that great when one looks at the rental costs of housing, even in places such as Toronto, Edmonton or Ottawa. Nonetheless, if people are being told that the accommodation which they

December 16, 1986
Income Tax Act
have, which may be quite modest, as a great deal of accommodation is in northern Canada, will have to be charged to them at $1,000, $1,200 or $1,500 a month, then they literally might not be able to afford to stay. Clearly, that would not be the intention in this case and that would definitely be unjust.
We have a situation where a number of the employees who were affected, including the trade union members referred to by the Hon. Member for Western Arctic (Mr. Nickerson), have previously benefited from tax free housing. It was not entered into their taxable income, they received it for free, and did not have to pay tax on the benefit. Of course, it was unfair that they received that free and others who had to pay their own rent did not get some equivalent concession. That is being addressed right now.
But if the housing in Pine Point, or in some other mining property in northern Canada is now to be valued at a very high level, these employees may find that they are worse off than if this present situation had prevailed. We have gone from being unfair to people who did not have a trade union contract, to being unfair to people who do have it and have traditionally had housing provided as part of their union contract. I would ask the Minister to address that particular point.
I agree with the point raised by the Hon. Member for Western Arctic in his amendment. I do not recall that was brought before us in the committee, where it may have had a good chance of being accepted before it came here. I hope that the Government in good faith would accept the points made by the Hon. Member for Western Arctic.
We will support Motion No. 4. I wish to put it to the Minister that the Department and the Department of Revenue Canada can surely accept the good faith of northerners and accept the fact that we are not talking about the business conditions and the size of business organizations that exist in southern Canada. After three or four years if it is found that there is some abuse taking place, then at that point some necessary measures can be taken. I suspect that the Hon. Member for Western Arctic would accept that. I believe that his approach is to begin on a good faith basis rather than to begin by suspecting that everybody who works for his brother-in-law is out to fiddle the tax system.
For those reasons, I would ask people to support Motion No. 4. Now that we have had an opportunity to address the general problems of Motion No. 5, I would support opposition to Motion No. 5 even though it was my colleagues and I who proposed it.

Mr. Speaker, the motions standing in my name deal with the alternative minimum tax. We have been advised in this House by the Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson) that the Government's purpose in introducing this Bill providing for an alternative minimum tax was to ensure that all taxpayers assume their fair share of the tax burden. In other words, each taxpayer-it is going to be extremely complicated-will have from now on to file in a regular income tax return, have a taxable income and pay so much income tax. If he has no income tax to pay, he will have, after submitting his return duly completed, to prepare another extremely complicated form to know whether he should pay an alternative minimum tax.
Mr. Speaker, for a Government which wanted to simplify our tax legislation, I can assure you that this Bill is a flop.
The fact remains that on this side of the House, we were and still are in favour of the principle of a minimum income tax as suggested by the Leader of our party during the election campaign. We thought that the Government was serious about wanting to make sure that no one, especially people on high incomes, would be able to get away with paying hardly any income tax to the federal or provincial governments.
Mr. Speaker, that was the objective, and we were all for it. However, Bill C-23 which introduces this minimum tax includes provisions with so many loopholes that no one will have to pay the minimum tax. For instance, a person who has to pay a minimum income tax of 17 per cent will be able to recover that amount over the next seven years if during that time, his regular income tax is high enough to preclude his paying a minimum tax. In other words, a person who has to pay minimum income tax has seven years in which to recover the extra amount paid. I don't see why it is necessary to make our tax system so complex, if the initial objective was to levy a minimum income tax.
Mr. Speaker, the purpose of Motion No. 7 is to reduce the recovery period from seven to three years. We think this is far
The Senate
more reasonable and that if the Government accepted our motion, it would have a minimum income tax with teeth. Otherwise this is going to be a pretty toothless proposition, and no one will feel the bite. In a number of articles written by tax experts, I found one author who said-I'm not sure whether I can find the exact quote-that the only good thing that could be said about the minimum tax was that in the final instance, no one would have to pay because of all the loopholes, and I think that if the Conservative Government is at all responsible, it should at least go along with Motion No. 7 and reduce the recovery period from seven to three years. Otherwise, this will just be a big joke.
The other motion, Motion No. 14 which has been regrouped with No. 7 for the purposes of debate, will remove a small subsection, Sub-section (3) at Clause 51, by striking out line 33 at page 96 and replacing it with more or less the same thing except for the number three in brackets. This is another loophole we want to close. Mr. Speaker, the Conservative Government has introduced a minimum income tax in an attempt to catch all the tax loopholes and tax shelters and tax evasion. The only exception will be capital gains.
I think it is grossly unfair to have this double standard for taxpayers. If we want to impose a minimum income tax, it should apply to all tax loopholes and not just to a few. I therefore recommend that these two motions be adopted, Mr. Speaker.

subtopic: PRIVATE MEMBERS' BUSINESS-MOTIONS   THE SENATE SUGGESTED EQUAL PROVINCIAL AND TERRITORIAL ELECTED REPRESENTATION
PRIVATE MEMBERS' BUSINESS-MOTIONS   THE SENATE SUGGESTED EQUAL PROVINCIAL AND TERRITORIAL ELECTED REPRESENTATION
speechtext:
That, in the opinion of this House, the Government should consider the advisability of introducing the appropriate measures to abolish the Senate and create a new Senate composed of Senators elected by the people of Canada on the basis of equal representation for each province and territory, and to initiate discussions to that end with provincial and territorial Governments at the earliest opportunity.
He said: Mr. Speaker, I have great pleasure in moving the motion before the House. What the motion wants is an efficient Senate elected by the people, with equal representation from each province and territory.
The report of the Special Joint Committee of the Senate and of the House of Commons on Senate Reform dated January, 1984 called for an elected Senate. The first statement in the report, Chapter 1, reads as follows:

December 16, 1986
The Senate
We have concluded that the Canadian Senate should be elected directly by the people of Canada.
An appointed Senate no longer meets the needs of the Canadian federation. An elected Senate is the only kind of Senate that can adequately fill what we think should be its principal role-the role of regional representations.
Because of the limited time allowed, I will deal only briefly with the matter of electing a Senate. However, I want to point out that the House of Commons is elected on the basis of population. Consequently, Ontario and Quebec, the two central provinces, will for a long, long time have a majority in the House of Commons. This is proper as representation in the House of Commons should be and is based on population. "Rep by pop" was fought for and won. It is an accepted rule for electing Members of Parliament.
When it comes to the Senate, however, there is no reason at all why the number of Senators should be based on population. Senators appointed now, whether for service to a political Party or on the basis of merit, may feel responsible to the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) or to the Government which appointed them but they are really accountable to no one. Our contention is that Senators would be elected by the people, so they will be responsible and accountable for their actions to the people who elected them.
The second requirement of the motion is that an equal number of Senators be elected from each province. I suggest five, with two from each territory until they attain provincial status. Each province would be divided into the appropriate number of regions or the Senators could be elected at large, and nominations would proceed according to the Elections Act.
While the Special Committee on Senate Reform recommended that Senators be elected, it then suggested that the Senate should be increased from 104 Members to 144 Members, with Quebec and Ontario retaining 24 Senators each. Assuming my recommendation of five Senators being elected from each province and two from each territory, the distribution as it is now, as it would be with 144 Senators and with equal representation from each province, would be as per the table included in my notes.
Taking the table as read-and I hope it will be included in Hansard-let us analyse the recommendations of the joint committee with regard to distribution. First, the distribution is at least partly based on population. For example, Prince Edward Island is given six Senators, while the other maritime provinces and the four western provinces get 12 and Ontario and Quebec retain 24. Surely P.E.I. being a province it is entitled to the same benefits as other provinces. The report rationalizes this by saying that if P.E.I. was given 12 Senators, then five provinces with as little as 13.4 per cent of Canada's population would have a majority of seats if they had the support of the territories. It is strange.
The House of Commons generally has 60 per cent of its Members from the Provinces of Ontario and Quebec, with only 28 per cent from the West and the North and about 12 per cent from the Atlantic provinces. That appears okay, but population should not be a factor at all in selecting Senators.
The selection should be on the basis of having the status of a province. The distribution of Senators by the special committee would really retain the status quo and would solve nothing. It might just a well stay as it is if all we are to accomplish is more expenditure from the people. Reform would be meaningless with Quebec and Ontario retaining 24 Senators and all other provinces with fewer seats. Ontario and Quebec already have a majority of Members in the House of Commons. Why should they also control the Senate? This motion will be fair to all provinces; each and every one will have equal power, with none having more power than any other.
However, how much would people have to pay for all this? The 144 Senators would increase the cost of the Senate in wages plus the tax-free allowance from about $6 million per year to almost $9 million. On the other hand, by having five Senators elected from each province, with two from the Yukon and two from the Northwest Territories, it would cut the cost in half and bring it down, in wages and cost of living, to less than $4 million, to say nothing about the tremendous reduction in the cost of offices and office expenses for staff, travelling, et cetera. If money means anything-and it means a lot to Canadian taxpayers-the triple E Senate would save millions. In addition, the real benefit and advantage would be that Senators would be accountable to the people who elected them, not to the Prime Minister nor the Goverment which appointed them.
An elected Senate, at least to start with, should continue to have the power extended to it by the Constitution Act, 1867. It should be noted that the absolute veto over legislation presently in effect has not been used once during the last 25 years.
I will now deal briefly with some concerns arising out of changes which will have to be made to the Constitution Act, 1867. Will huge sums of money have to be paid to present Senators allegedly because of dismissal? The Constitution Act, 1867 sets out the method of selection, the retirement age, and certain circumstances under which a person who is summoned to the Senate is disqualified from membership. An amendment would be necessary when the Senate is either abolished or a new method of selection is implemented.
Some may argue, as did the report of the joint committee on Senate reform, that there is some constitutional commitment by the Government to those Senators appointed for life or until age 75. When the Constitution was amended to change the senatorial term from life to retirement at age 75, legislation then gave an option to those in the Senate who had reached the age of 75 years either to continue or to retire with a pension. This option was given, but it could have retired them all over or under the age of 75.
In terms of compensation, why would Senators not be treated the same as other Canadians who lose their jobs or retire? Pensions are earned through contributions which persons make to a fund, as in industry. Senators who have spent some years in the Senate would secure a pension based on their years of service and their contributions. It would mean that they would secure the amount which they had properly
December 16, 1986

earned under the Act under which they worked, as do workers under UIC and workers under Canada Pension. It is the same for Members of Parliament who are defeated in an election or retire. Why should Senators be treated differently from other Canadians?
Section 42(l)(b) of the Constitution Act, 1982 specifically states that any change in the powers of the Senate must be accomplished by means of the general amending formula. However, this could be done without the consent of the Senate. Presumably such an amendment would simply repeal Section 26 which gives the Government the right to appoint additional Senators in order to break a deadlock in the House of Commons. The section dealing with retirement at age 75 would be dropped as well. The constitutional amendment would provide the method of election, and the mechanics would be left to be inserted in the Canada Elections Act.
If the Senate refuses to pass such an amendment, does the House of Commons have any recourse? A constitutional amendment which would either abolish the Senate or change the method of selection to popular election would have to be accomplished by the utilization of the general amending formula, which allows approval by the central Government and two-thirds of the provinces. This being the case, Senate approval is not required if within 180 days of the amendment being first passed by the House of Commons the Senate refuses to act or acts in a negative fashion. The matter is simply re-enacted by the House of Commons.
I submit that if the Senate is not reformed, it may well mean that the Canada we love may not for long be the Canada we know and have today. In other words, the salvation of Canada as we know it, with its varying climates, its varying regions, and its many people, is tied in to a large degree with providing protection for all regions, which in turn requires this fundamental reform of the Senate. A new Senate responsible to the people will take a sober second look at legislation to ensure that every part of Canada has an opportunity to grow and to retain its culture and language. It will also ensure that every region is treated fairly and that people in every part of the country have an equal chance to enjoy the benefits of our nation.
The bottom line in the discussion of the motion is fairness to all parts of Canada. By passing all stages it will tell Canadians that the Government of Canada and the House of Commons have listened and are acting on their message and that every region will be treated fairly, whether it be the far East, the far South, or in the centre.
I urge all Hon. Members to support the motion. The failure of the motion to pass could mean a shocking catastrophe.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I find myself in the strange but certainly welcome position of totally agreeing with the Hon. Member for Bow
The Senate
River (Mr. Taylor) and complimenting him on his resolution. Let me say to him that we are prepared to lend our support to an important and worth-while initiative.
I would like to point out to the House that at the recent national policy convention held some three weeks ago, delegates overwhelmingly supported this proposal to include an elected Senate that was equal and had additional powers granted to it so that it could become a Chamber of substantial weight and effectiveness in representing regional interests in Canada. To my knowledge, it is the only time that a major national Party in Canada has gone on record fully endorsing and supporting the concept of an elected and equal Senate. I have no problem in putting forward that notion.
I would like to talk about why it must be done and why Members of this House have an opportunity at this time to show some real leadership in responding to an egregious sense of grievance in many parts of Canada and to recognize that in effect our constitutional system is incomplete. We have the only federal system in the world that does not have a second Chamber that effectively represents regional interests on the basis of democratic accountability. It is not my job to second-guess the wisdom of the confederation of our forefathers. By making the decision as they did at that time to have a Senate that is an appointed body and having that tradition maintained has resulted in a situation that while the Senate does useful work-and there are some very fine people in the Senate-it does not carry the heft, the leverage or the balance within the system of making decisions required to ensure for people in regions not concentrated with high levels of economic or political power that they will get a fair deal. As a result, there are too many examples over too much of our history where decisions have been made not on the basis of fairness but on the basis of political weight.
I recall the famous statement of Napoleon who once said to the Pope: "Where are your battalions?" That is too often a question raised in our system of decision making. The counterbalances we have, the Cabinet system and the federal-provincial conferences, are not in themselves sufficient to give the kind of forum for debate and discussion and the sense of security and confidence on the part of individuals in places like western Canada and the Atlantic to be heard effectively.
There is no doubt this issue of an elected equal Senate has gained a great deal of importance and an incredible sense of urgency because of the recent decisions by the Conservative Government on the CF-18 matter. I can think of no matter, certainly in my living memory, which has struck so deeply into the consciousness and psyche of westerners than that decision. People saw by all the reasonable rational criteria that an important contract should have been awarded to western Canada but was not because of interference in the system. One can only judge by statements made by Ministers of the Crown opposite that it was done purely to meet some political requirements in central Canada. That is not acceptable. Westerners will not continue to accept that situation. I do not say that partisanly because these situations can happen with

December 16, 1986
The Senate
all Governments. I think westerners have had it with CF-18 decisions. They will no longer accept that kind of bias and discriminatory decision-making. Westerners want to be sure that they have an equal chance to have their voices heard and an equal chance to ensure that there is political balance.
A week or so after the CF-18 decision was announced I happened to be in my home riding of Winnipeg watching the congressional election returns coming in from the State of North Dakota. It was intriguing to see the President of the United States having to pay as much attention to the election of Senators from North and South Dakota as he did about an election of a Senator from California and New York. There is no question that the calculation going into the political process in the United States must be duplicated here in some way.
I think the Hon. Member for Bow River has illustrated the various ways in which the so-called technical problems can be overcome. I am not saying that I adhere totally to the position he has put forward in terms of the exact model, but this motion represents a first step in this House of Commons in coming to grips with the issue.
I decry in part the reaction that we had in this House a year or so ago when the then Minister of Justice brought in a Senate Bill that was about taking the powers of the Senate away. It was supported by the New Democrats who said they wanted to abolish the Senate, therefore totally depriving the regions of any fair degree of representation. This is a chance to redress that kind of silliness and show people in the other parts of the country that we mean business.

Mr. Speaker, I think it is imperative that all Members from all regions of Canada understand and support this motion, because it is a very important initiative which attests to the interest of all Members from coast to coast in extending fair treatment to people in western Canada and the Maritimes. This is a great opportunity to show unity in this country.
I urge my colleagues and other Members to support the motion of the Hon. Member for Bow river (Mr. Taylor).

I rise because I think this is one of the most important debates and one of the most important resolutions that has ever been presented in this House. I think the Member for Bow River put it correctly that unless Members of Parliament take this kind of initiative, unless we show some leadership in this very crucial issue, there will be an increasing sense of alienation, scepticism and an increasing sense that the system does not work for large sections of the country. We see that situation increasingly where the economy of this country is becoming a split level economy. As we shift from a commodity resource base into an industry that is based upon services, information and research, the concentration of economic power becomes more consolidated in southern parts of Ontario and the St. Lawrence mainland. The only way one can provide a counterbalance to that is through the political system. The only way you can ensure a fair distribution of the economic
gains in this country is to ensure it through the distribution of the federal system. If the federal system is flawed and if there is a major weakness in that system, if structurally it is not able to ensure the balance wheel constantly in operation, then there will not be that sense of confidence about being able to receive a fair deal and a fair reception of the growth and prosperity of Canada. We are in danger of having a split-level society, a country that finds itself divided.
I can only say that while this is not the total panacea, symbolically and in a very conscious way, this is an important demonstration of the willingness of the country to take a good look at itself, to realize that the evolution of our Constitution is not by any means over, and that the kind of good, honest outpouring of feeling exhibited in this House in the past to our colleagues from Quebec when they had grievances on language and culture must now be demonstrated by our colleagues from Quebec and Ontario on this issue that is so crucial and important to the West and the Maritimes.
There have been times when this House has shown an incredible generosity of spirit in recognizing that there has to be some limitation on one's rights in order to better the rights of others. That is how a civilized society operates. This House has demonstrated that in the past when we were threatened with separation over questions of language and culture. We now have the same kind of threat in the form of unfair distribution of economic and political power.
I suggest to you and all other Members of this House that this resolution provides an answer to that problem. It therefore deserves a proper review by this House. That will demonstrate that we are not blind to the difficulties we face, that in fact we are prepared to look at them collectively because we realize that the House of Commons has a responsibility to all of Canada.

subtopic: PRIVATE MEMBERS' BUSINESS-MOTIONS   THE SENATE SUGGESTED EQUAL PROVINCIAL AND TERRITORIAL ELECTED REPRESENTATION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, like the previous speaker, I want to commend the Hon. Member for Bow River (Mr. Taylor) for his initiative in introducing this subject in the House. As it is now constituted, the Senate has no place in a democracy. My reason for saying that is that we have a legislative Chamber without a mandate from the people. That, in the 20th century, is the only basis for legislative authority. We no longer recognize divine right, aristocratic superiority or any other consideration in a democracy except one, that of a mandate from the people in a free and democratic election.
Without calling into question the personal virtues or merit of members of the other place, we have to face the reality expressed in that sorry, inexcusable vacuity of authority because of which the Senate is unable to function as a true legislature. It has become a kind of legislative refinery whose chief positive role is to improve this or that feature of a Bill sent to it by the House of Commons. It has ceased to function as a legislature in the way originally intended. It is for that reason that opinion on all sides of the House over the years has
December 16, 1986

supported the intent of this motion before us. For example, in 1965 the Hon. Stanley Knowles told the House:
We ought to ask ourselves whether there is any place in our parliamentary institution for a group of people who are not responsible to the electors.
That is the key. If you would be a legislature today, you must be accountable to the electors. You must receive from them that confidence which gives us authority to act. Another member of the other place, Senator Michael Pitfield, said:
As an appointed Chamber it simply does not carry the credibility to perform the role in this day and age.
That is the point. We need to have an elected Senate if it is to justify its position as an upper House.
Regardless of the quality of the people who comprise it, and there is no question about that in this debate, it cannot, as an appointed Chamber, function with the full scope of an elected House. It does not usually initiate Bills of its own. It seldom dares to veto Bills from this House. It almost never goes beyond the function of refining something by rubbing off this rough edge or polishing up that dullness. However, that is surely not enough to justify it being the upper House of this Parliament. It purports to be an upper House but it lacks that essential without which it cannot function as an upper House.
The Hon. Robert L. Stanfield, with the great wisdom and perspicacity with which we associate him, has said:
We should do whatever is in our power to increase its credibility, and that has to come basically through reform of the appointment process.
What better reform than to make it an elected Chamber? Some 25 years ago the need for some such solution was signalled in the words of the Right Hon. Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Turner) when he said:
The Senate, in terms of current facts, no longer plays a part in the government of Canada.
That is the view of the Leader of the Liberal Party. The Senate no longer plays a part in the Government of Canada. The Hon. Member who introduced this motion identified the reason. It is not because individual members lack ability or dedication. It is because they lack a mandate from the people which only an election can give them.
I submit that the question is: Do we want an elected upper House? Or, do we want a single Chamber Parliament? There is no place in the 20th century for an appointed upper House. Democracy around the world demonstrates that there is a place for an elected upper House. The variations found in such democracies as West Germany, France, the U.S., Italy and Australia, to name only a few, demonstrate that. Therefore, I join with those who support this motion to bring before the people of Canada and their representatives the need for a profound transformation in the character and structure of the upper House of this Parliament. In that way it can perform its function in a way appropriate to this century and the one which lies ahead.
I would ask that the mover of the motion consider some emendation of the second part of his motion. I am thinking of the assumptions that underlie the call for equal representation
The Senate
of every province and territory without regard to population. The difficulties are obvious. We all know we have one province with only 125,000 people, another province with over six million people, and a third province with more than 8.5 million people. We must consider not removing the disproportionate character of this country and what that requires simply by saying we have provided for it in the House of Commons. We do not remove it by pointing to the way in which the U.S. Senate has equal representation for each state, whether it be Rhode Island or California. Doing that ignores the proportion of population among the regions and divisions of Canada. Ontario represents 35 per cent of the people of this country. There is no state in the Union that represents 35 per cent of the people of the U.S. If there was, it would have a population of 75 million and include not only California with its 25 million but most of the states west of the Mississippi River. If a state like that existed, then you would begin to see what it means to say "we only have two Senators from California". The same thing applies to the Province of Quebec in proportion, indeed every province. I am not asking for representation by population in the Senate such as we have in the House. We should have something which is uniquely Canadian and not a simplistic attempt to duplicate what they have in the U.S.
In this country, in addition to provinces and territories, we have four or five recognizable regions. We should think in terms of allotting each of those regions a more or less equal representation so there would be a strong voice from the underpopulated parts of Canada such as the Atlantic Provinces and the Prairies. We would have a strong voice from the North out of proportion to the number of its people, but we would not have the hopeless and, I submit, unacceptable situation of having equal representation from each province and each territory.
I do not suggest this simply to speak against the motion but, rather, to raise a question. When this motion proceeds, as I hope it will, and is considered by the Government and again by the House in the form of a Bill, I ask that we consider the problem which I have identified and which I believe requires careful reflection by committee and the House. The motion before us is meritorious and requires further reflection by Parliament and, ultimately, action by us all.

Mr. Speaker, I am very pleased to join today's debate on the motion introduced by my colleague from Bow River (Mr. Taylor). If I may continue along the lines of the remarks made by my colleague from Scarborough West (Mr. Stackhouse), I would say we have before us a motion which is full of good ideas and which points the way towards a future which will be more progressive and more democratic than our present institutions. Still, Mr. Speaker, my Party and I can see the shortcomings of this motion.

December 16, 1986
The Senate
We are talking about a non-democratic institution-as others have described it-at the very core of our democratic legislative process. In other words, there is an obvious contradiction in terms with our legislative institutions and this very Parliament.
Mr. Speaker, we now find ourselves in a situation where we have a House of Commons elected by the people, where every sitting Member was given a mandate by his or her electors. But we also have the other place-like my colleagues I would not want to criticize those who sit there now-we have in the other place a House where the right to sit comes only and exclusively from this Government. To put it another way, the present Government could use the Senate to reward its friends and, in light of what is now going on, to reward those who have been the good and faithful servants of the country, but especially those who belong to the Government Party.
And I myself, Mr. Speaker, have friends in the Senate. There are senators whom, I say it frankly, I admire, but what the Senate institution stands for is the patronage system that is imbedded in the Government, and the Government is always tempted to use that system despite its past protests, to try and turn it to its own purposes. And that kind of Senate subservience, that kind of departure from the concept of a true Senate as it should be, along the lines of the Roman model, and that deterioration started under the previous Government, the Trudeau Liberal Government. It was during that time that the nefarious practice of using Senate appointments to set up an election team, an election planning team within Parliament itself, a team that is there for the one and only purpose of partisan politics.
This is a corruption of the Parliamentary system for which our friends on the Liberal benches should apologize to the nation, and even for having corrupted the senators. Unfortunately, that system of corruption kept on under this Government, which has used not all but some appointments to install its own election committees at the Senate level. Therefore, Mr. Speaker, this is an ill-prepared legislation, involving a mere improvement on matters of detail over the present Senate. There are serious gaps in a proposal that would replace the present Senate by an elected Senate. I say it quite frankly, Mr. Speaker, I am a one-Chamber man myself, and our party's policies adopted in convention are for one chamber only. We believe that a single chamber is the choice of the majority of Canadians themselves. I know I will probably be repeating what has been said by the Hon. Member for Scarborough West (Mr. Stackhouse).
The main gaps in the concept of an equal, elected, efficient Senate, as it is often mentioned in the headlines, is that of course proportional representation exists in the House of Commons, but that is a proportional system that is based of course on the size of the various constituencies. Electoral boundaries have been changed according to history, tradition. There is that imbalance on which everyone will agree. There are, for instance, in Ontario constituencies, and I believe that
even includes Scarborough, that have a larger population than the whole of Prince Edward Island. There were constituencies in other provinces that were larger for instance than my own, larger than the whole of Germany, 30 times larger geographically speaking than Prince Edward Island, but with only one Member to represent them, while there are now four in the example I am using. It is obvious, Mr. Speaker, that if we had agreed to the principle of an equal, effective, elected Senate, some people would have requested a reform of our system of representation in this House so that Members of Parliament could be elected strictly on the basis of the same number of people in each of our constituencies, which would naturally be against the legitimate interests of my constituents, who live in vast rural regions where there can be about 100 villages of which 30 cannot be reached by road. This means that if this Bill is passed, we shall have to consider changing our system of representation in this House.
As I have just said, Mr. Speaker, I am myself a unicameralist. I think that we should look at the examples before us. Many provinces began with two Houses, a non-elected Senate and an elected Chamber. Today, those provinces all have one Chamber, and I would even go as far as saying that those provincial Governments work better than the federal Government and are better able to meet the needs and aspirations of their voters. We also have the example of our large municipalities, some of which represent over 10 per cent of our population, and which are always unicameral. There are difficulties in implementing this Bill which must be mentioned, Mr. Speaker because, ever since the adoption of the Canadian Constitution we have had a consultation process which should come into play before this kind of measure can be passed.
Then there is the fact that our native people represent the two major immigration races or, as someone said, the founding nations.
On what basis would a triple E Senate represent the great concept we have of our founding races and our native people?
Naturally, Mr. Speaker, I may be somewhat disappointed to see that the motion of my colleague from Bow River (Mr. Taylor) has been chosen as a votable item instead of mine which was picked first.
Once again, Mr. Speaker, I must conclude that the real solution, the solution which meets the needs of all Canadians, is the unicameral solution where there is no room for a Senate.
