Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to speak to this motion introduced by the Hon. Member for Bow River (Mr. Taylor) urging the House to endorse a proposal to abolish the existing Senate and create a new Senate-elected this time-where provinces and territories would have equal representation.
I take this opportunity to point out that the Hon. Member for Bow River will soon be celebrating his 40 years as an elected politician-elected, I repeat-and I should think this is the appropriate time in this debate to quote the great principle
December 16, 1986

which prevailed when the United States of America were founded, the famous words of Thomas Payne:
One cannot tax people without being duly elected. And 1 think the House will agree that one of the few people who today would be worthy to belong to the Senate is our hon. friend from Bow River who has been re-elected for forty years.
Imagine! He has been elected so many times there would be every justification, no offence intended, to give him a seat in the Senate without the benefit of election. And I would have no trouble supporting such a proposal. He has successfully faced the electorate so many times, both in the provincial legislature and in the House, that I think he and other people like him should be the first to be given a seat in the Senate.
"No taxation without representation".

That is the basic principle behind this motion to abolish the Senate, which, it has to be said, is a bit of an anachronism. I may recall that last year, our hon. friends in the other place obstructed the passage of Bill C-11 for several weeks. This was a Bill to provide borrowing authority for the new Government, a Government that had been elected with an exceptional and indeed historic majority. And the Senate obstructed this legislation. Why? In any case, the Liberal Senators were opposed to adopting and ratifying a Bill that constituted a major borrowing authority, the result being to create uncertainty on the financial markets and even raise doubts internationally, at a time when our dollar was more or less sagging. This situation was created by people who were not elected and who were taking this opportunity to ridicule the elected Members of Parliament who had been unanimous in adopting this Bill.
So we have the whole contradiction of this second Chamber that is applying a kind of veto, theoretically at least, but in this particular case a very real veto, to the decisions of the elected representatives of the people of Canada.
I and many of my colleagues find the situation particularly unacceptable. I may recall that the issue of the legitimacy and accountability of members of the Senate has been raised before in the course of history and as recently as last year, with these important people who, being appointed, are responsible to no one, and I tend to agree with the Hon. Member for the New Democratic Party whom I wish to congratulate on addressing the House in French, thus enhancing the francophone presence in this Chamber, and I would say that the Hon. Member is making a very valuable contribution in this respect, and I was going to say that the Hon. Member stressed the patronage aspect of these appointments, and so forth.
I would not go that far. I believe there are senators who are doing exceptional work here in Ottawa. Most of them, Mr. The Senate
Speaker, are hard workers and are active on various committees, and they express views that reflect their wisdom and experience. But they still have this major drawback that they are not elected and are accountable to no one.
And when they decide-as was the case of the Liberal senators-to obstruct the decisions of a Government that was elected with such a broad majority by the Canadian people, it is time to start asking some very serious questions. And perhaps we should take this proposal by the Hon. Member who has such broad parliamentary experience as an opportunity to review this issue.

this debate can lead to challenging and worthy considerations. subtopic: PRIVATE MEMBERS' BUSINESS-MOTIONS   THE SENATE SUGGESTED EQUAL PROVINCIAL AND TERRITORIAL ELECTED REPRESENTATION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it gives me pleasure today to rise in the debate on the motion of our colleague for Bow River (Mr. Taylor). The same motion has been introduced on numerous occasions in the past, perhaps not in this specific form, but at least in its general principle.
First, Mr. Speaker, I must explain my own position. I am in favour of an elected Senate. Second, however, I disagree with the suggestion that there should be an identical number of representatives from each province in the other Chamber. In my opinion, there should be an equal number of representatives from each region. Naturally, we would then have to decide whether there would be four regions, five regions, or whatever. We shall come back to this later.
I really take objection to the view of some Hon. Members that Canada should have a unicameral federal Parliament. I totally disagree with that idea. I just cannot understand why we would ever threaten the other House with abolition even when we disagree with it. It has been stated often that we do not need a second legislature. I believe that to suggest that is wrong and does not recognize some of the history of our country.
At Confederation there were really two roles identified for our Senate. The first role was to review the legislation. I think most people would agree that the Senate has done that job reasonably well. The second role of the upper Chamber, as I understand it, is to represent the regions of our country. At that time there were three regions; Canada East, Canada West-later to be called Quebec and Ontario-and the Maritimes. It was the wish of the Fathers of Confederation that one third of the Senators would come from the Province of Canada East or from the Province of Quebec. The reason for that was to recognize the principle of the two founding nations. That is why it is important to keep an upper House and to keep it representative of the regions of our country. The Senators, of course, presently represent their respective provinces except the Senators who represent the Province of Quebec, who are also, of course, representatives of a given
area, a Senate riding, if you wish, or a seigneurie, based on the historical antecedents prior to the active union of 1840 and, indeed, in large measure prior to the Constitutional Act of 1791.

Mr. Speaker, the Conservative Government elected in 1979 did not have enough elected Members in this House to represent effectively the Quebec population. Under the circumstances, one of the founding nations could have run the risk of not being represented at all in that government. Fortunately, at the time, there was a Senate. The Prime Minister of the day, who is now Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Clark) went to the Senate in search of people whom he deemed competent to represent the region of Quebec and the founding nation made up of francophones and managed to appoint a Cabinet which included representatives of that group.
Let us imagine an assembly made up of a single House facing the same situation! Naturally, we would have had a Cabinet with very few Quebec or francophones representatives in the Ministry, if at all, because we know that there were only two PC Members out of 75 representing Quebec, and only one a Francophone. That did not represent the group.
If I am saying that, it is because an NDP Member said a while ago that he was in favour of a single House; I feel such a proposition could not apply to our country, because it is important to have an assembly or Parliament made up of two houses.

To the extent that we must continue to have a bicameral House, I agree with the Hon. Member opposite. To the extent Senators should be elected, I agree. To the extent that each should represent a given area of our country, I also agree. I suppose the only point I disagree with is that the Hon. Member opposite is saying they should be elected in exactly the same number for each province. I say that that idea does not recognize the two founding nations principle of our country and it does not recognize certain historical antecedents.
As stated by the Hon. Member for Scarborough West (Mr. Stackhouse), the formula that the Hon. Member for Bow River (Mr. Taylor) is using resembles the American formula, with the same number of Senators per state. However, in the United States there is not one state, one province or one jurisdiction which has 35 per cent of the population. In this country there is such a province.
I am not saying that the Senate should have a number of seats which is proportional to its population, because then effectively we would have areas of our country which would be almost totally devoid of representation. I do not think we should use the representation by population principle nor the identical number per province principle, but, rather, a marriage of both, which is effectively what the regional principle is. In other words, the division of the total number of Senators should be based on various regions of our country. I
December 16, 1986

know there is still debate going on as to whether our country has four regions or five. Mr. Yurko, the former Hon. Member for Edmonton East, addressed that subject extensively in the past. We have had a lot of constructive debate, but the issue has not been totally solved.
With that I will end my remarks and say that in my view the motion of the Hon. Member has a great deal of merit. I congratulate him for bringing it forward. I hope that if it goes to committee we can amend it somewhat in order to reflect the principle that I have outlined. I hope that the day will come soon when we will stop talking about reforming the Senate and actually do it.
